documents.abstract: Text, images, audio, touch, and even robot actions can, in principle, all be rendered onto a single canvas, suggesting an ambitious goal of unifying all modalities within vision. Language provides the natural first test. To subsume it, a visual model must reason directly over text in pixels. Across a wide range of image, video, and unified multimodal generators, however, we find that their visual generation modules cannot perform symbolic reasoning over text on the canvas. They succeed only when an underlying text module or prompt rewriter already supplies the answer, effectively reducing the generator to a mere renderer, a limitation that post-training does little to resolve. To test whether this failure stems from pixels themselves or from current training paradigms, we train a family of purely pixel-space generative models from scratch without any text pathway. With images as their sole input and output, these models read questions, write intermediate steps, and produce answers directly on the canvas. Remarkably, they exhibit hallmark behaviors of large language models. Performance improves predictably with scale following a power law. Writing intermediate steps frame by frame substantially outperforms single-frame answering, echoing chain-of-thought, while reinforcement-learning post-training further strengthens reasoning. Moreover, sharing one canvas allows the same model to reason across modalities, a capability that text-only language models lack. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of these phenomena in purely pixel-space generative models free of text tokens.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) seeks to enhance the transparency and accountability of machine learning systems, yet most methods follow a one-size-fits-all paradigm that neglects user differences in expertise, goals, and cognitive needs. Although Large Language Models can translate technical explanations into natural language, they introduce challenges related to faithfulness and hallucinations. To address these challenges, we present PONTE ( P ersonalized O rchestration for N atural language T rustworthy E xplanations), a human-in-the-loop framework for adaptive and reliable XAI narratives. PONTE models personalization as a closed-loop validation and adaptation process rather than prompt engineering. It combines: (i) a low-dimensional preference model capturing stylistic requirements; (ii) a preference-conditioned generator grounded in structured XAI artifacts; and (iii) verification modules enforcing numerical faithfulness, informational completeness, and stylistic alignment, optionally supported by retrieval-grounded argumentation. User feedback iteratively updates the preference state, enabling quick personalization. Automatic and human evaluations across healthcare and finance domains show that the verification–refinement loop substantially improves completeness and stylistic alignment over validation-free generation. Human studies further confirm strong agreement between intended preference vectors and perceived style, robustness to generation stochasticity, and consistently positive quality assessments.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Practice-Dependent Development of Discernment, an account of how repeated practice with correction can develop a capacity to discriminate that receiving a statement once does not secure. Retained wording, correct performance on practiced cases, and transferable discernment are separate achievements. The account assesses discernment through demonstrated discrimination across specified new cases, with the conditions of practice and feedback recorded. Exposure to a rule, repetition, and success on familiar examples do not alone establish transfer. Statements can accelerate learning and sometimes do much of the work that practice would otherwise do, while repetition without correction can entrench error. The assessment asks what was stated, what was practiced, how errors were corrected, and whether performance transfers under the conditions in which the capacity will be used. The discussion sets the mechanism beside Ericsson, Krampe, and Tesch-Römer’s account of deliberate practice and examines two documented cases. Tanaka, Curran, and Sheinberg’s 2005 bird-identification study compared species-level and family-level training with equal exposure and corrective feedback. The species-level advantage transferred to new photographs of trained species; for entirely new species, it was significant for wading birds but not owls. Accounts of Nainoa Thompson’s training under Mau Piailug and the 1980 voyages of Hōkūle‘a trace the development of wayfinding through corrected practice at sea. Piailug made decisive interventions on the outbound passage. On the return, Thompson made most navigational decisions while his teacher remained aboard but largely kept out of the navigation. Part of the Relational Conditions and Dynamics series within On Human Modeling, the paper examines who arranges practice, supplies correction, defines adequate discernment, and tests transfer. Potential applications in human–AI research include tutoring, training design, and competence assessment that distinguish repeating a rule or succeeding on familiar tasks from discriminating correctly in new cases under specified conditions.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: Background/Aims Despite the increasing endoscopic volume and complexity in Korea, comprehensive data on the musculoskeletal health of gastrointestinal endoscopists remains limited. This study examined the prevalence, risk factors, and interventions related to musculoskeletal pain in Korea. Methods A nationwide cross-sectional web survey was conducted in November 2023. We analyzed responses from 209 endoscopists regarding demographics, practice patterns, symptoms, and ergonomic behaviors using multivariate logistic regression to identify factors associated with musculoskeletal pain. Results Among the respondents, 72.2% reported musculoskeletal pain, most frequently in the hand/wrist/fingers (57.4%) and shoulders (51.7%). Objective workload showed an apparent threshold-like pattern associated with the overall pain (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 2.18 for high workload; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.09–4.36). In contrast, perceived procedural burden was a robust independent predictor for both overall pain (aOR, 2.29; 95% CI, 1.50–3.50) and site-specific pain, particularly the neck (aOR, 1.88) and hand/wrist/fingers (aOR, 1.71). While 42.1% used general ergonomic aids, 70.3% expressed willingness to adopt endoscopy-specific devices. Conclusions Musculoskeletal pain is prevalent among endoscopists in Korea. Objective workload was associated with overall pain susceptibility, showing a threshold-like pattern, whereas perceived procedural burden was independently associated with both overall and site-specific symptoms. These findings highlight the need for targeted ergonomic interventions and endoscopy-specific technologies.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Standardized preprocessing has transformed human neuroimaging into a reproducible, population-scale enterprise, yet equivalent computational frameworks for non-human primates (NHPs) remain absent, forcing continued reliance on fragmented, labor-intensive workflows. Here we introduce PrimateX, a multi-agentic computational framework in which LLM-guided orchestration dynamically routes structural MRI scans through species-tailored, topology-preserving workflows, extracting cortical surfaces directly from raw volumes with full provenance tracking across marmosets, macaques, chimpanzees, and humans. Validated on 1,221 NHP and 1,113 human scans, PrimateX outperformed existing NHP pipelines in segmentation and surface reconstruction while matching dedicated human tools such as FSL in their native domain. Through MRI-style data augmentation, the framework achieved robust zero-shot generalization to 8 unseen primate species across 31 cohorts from 19 global sites (n = 157). Critically, the routing architecture and closed-loop quality-control mechanisms, demonstrated through diverse downstream neuroimaging analyses and cross-species research, establish PrimateX as a widely-applicable computational paradigm. PrimateX is available at https://primatex.pku.edu.cn.

A single academic vacancy can draw hundreds of applications, and the first screening round consumes most of a committee's time. We describe a CV Priority Sorter deployed at a national platform for academic vacancies and integrated with its vacancy database. It proposes a reading order for a pile of CVs and leaves every decision to the committee, pairing a frozen multilingual transformer encoder with a per-session linear model that retrains after each label and is discarded when the session ends. It works: on a pool of 300 synthetic CVs, a committee reading in the tool's order reaches 95% of the relevant candidates after half the pile, where an arbitrary order needs almost all of it. This paper is about what we found when we audited that claim, rather than about the system itself. Three findings changed the product. The pool turned out to be sortable by document length alone, which makes precision-style metrics on it uninformative; regenerating it under a shared length budget removes that shortcut and leaves the reading-depth result standing. The four-level agreement score such systems report, ours included, is a binary probability cut at fixed thresholds, so it follows the classifier's confidence rather than its ranking and falls as labels accumulate. And uncertainty sampling, the obvious way to implement a "suggest the next CV" button, leaves model quality intact but raises the committee's total reading load above the no-label baseline, because the CVs it asks about are the ones that would otherwise be skipped. A fourth result shows where to look next: a hosted LLM embedding model lifts zero-label ordinal discrimination from 0.66 to 0.80 under length control, then stops mattering once the session model has two dozen labels; a local cross-encoder matches that cold-start gain without sending data out. We report the fixes each finding forced.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Relevance. The effectiveness of public administration in the sphere of security is determined not only by the resource capacity of individual security and defence sector actors, but primarily by the quality of their horizontal interaction under dynamic hybrid threats. The experience of repelling massed missile and drone strikes on Ukraine’s critical infrastructure in 2022–2024 has shown that departmental data fragmentation, functional duplication, and the absence of formalized interaction protocols among the intelligence community, civil protection forces, and critical infrastructure operators significantly reduce the speed and quality of administrative decisions. Aim. The article aims to diagnose the key problems of interagency coordination in the sphere of state security of Ukraine and to substantiate organizational mechanisms for solving them. Objectives: to identify typical determinants of interagency interaction inefficiency; to demonstrate, using the "detection – alerting – response" chain during massed strikes on energy infrastructure, how data fragmentation translates into a loss of response time; to develop the authors’ previously proposed resilience mechanisms into operational proposals; to assess the potential of existing digital situational-awareness platforms for expanding coordination beyond the military domain. Methods. Systemic and comparative analysis of foreign coordination models, case study, structural-logical modelling. Results. Five systemic determinants of coordination inefficiency were identified: hierarchy instead of networking; departmental data fragmentation; unformalized interaction protocols; legal gaps in the distribution of powers; and the absence of an institutionalized lessons-learned cycle. The case study demonstrated a gap between military intelligence information and civilian response. An organizational-legal mechanism for overcoming this gap is substantiated, based on extending the architecture of an existing situational-awareness platform to non-military coordination actors. Conclusions. Eliminating interagency fragmentation requires a shift from a hierarchical to a network-centric security governance model, the institutionalization of subsidiarity-based response protocols, and a legally embedded lessons-learned cycle.

Experiments show that generative AI raises productivity on specific tasks by 14 to 40 percent, but who benefits when it spreads through the economy is far less clear. This study builds a capture accounting from task to economy. It links published field and survey evidence on productivity gains, adoption and wage pass-through to an exact decomposition of productivity gains in the U.S. nonfarm business sector, using the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) release of 5 November 2026 and the Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey. Between the first quarter of 2024 and the third quarter of 2026, output per hour rose by 6.35 log points; 3.28 points (51.7 percent; rounding interval 50.3 to 53.1) reached workers as higher compensation relative to output prices, and 3.07 points went to nonlabor income as the labor share fell to 53.0 percent, the lowest since 1947. Labor’s capture fell from 84 percent in 2024 to 70 percent in 2025 and turned negative (-16 percent) in the four quarters to 2026 Q3, while nonfinancial corporate unit profits rose 16.1 percent. At the worker level, Danish administrative data show only 3 to 7 percent of productivity gains reaching earnings. A consistency bound combining these pass-through rates with plausible shares of AI in productivity growth implies that AI explains a minority of the rise in nonlabor capture (median 23 percent; 5th to 95th percentile 8 to 38 percent) and cannot be the whole story. The evidence is descriptive and aggregate, and the AI shares are bounds, not estimates. Purpose - This study asks who captures the economic gains from workplace AI, and how much of the recent shift in the distribution of productivity gains could plausibly be attributed to it. Design/methodology/approach - The paper combines published task-level, worker-level and firm-level evidence with an exact capture decomposition of BLS quarterly data, rounding-error Monte Carlo intervals, and a consistency analysis that bounds the AI contribution using pass-through rates and adoption arithmetic. Findings - Roughly half of the recent productivity gain went to workers and half to nonlabor income, with workers’ share falling over time and turning negative in the latest quarters. AI use is concentrated in large firms and in information and finance. Pass-through of AI-specific gains to workers is small, but AI can account for only a minority of the shift. Research limitations/implications - Aggregate indexes are rounded and revised, AI shares of productivity growth are not observed, and field studies are not representative of the economy. The analysis cannot identify causal effects. Practical implications - Bargaining institutions, training and transparency over how time savings are used are likely to determine capture, and policy should track labor’s share of gains alongside productivity. Social implications - Productivity growth need not translate into prosperity for workers, and young entrants in exposed occupations face distinct employment risk. Originality/value - The paper provides a transparent accounting that connects micro and macro evidence on AI’s distributional effects and quantifies what current data can and cannot say.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: Universal Design for Learning (UDL) offers a valuable framework for developing inclusive and accessible courses, but educators often receive limited support in translating its broad principles into context-specific teaching and assessment practices. This paper reports on the design of a custom generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) conversational assistant prototype developed to support computing educators in Australian tertiary education in applying UDL to their courses. The prototype provides concrete, non-directive suggestions across the three tenets of UDL, multiple means of engagement, representation, action and expression. Rather than treating GenAI as a generic automation tool, the prototype explores how prompt design, scope limitation, structured outputs, and persona-informed contexts can scaffold inclusive pedagogical reflection while maintaining academic judgement. The paper presents the functional prototype as its primary contribution and describes its design considerations, prompt architecture, and early scenario-based testing.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being considered as tools for computational social science, yet their implications for survey and public-opinion research remain insufficiently understood. This study examines whether and how they can serve as methodological instruments for estimating aggregate public opinion under out-of-sample conditions. Across three studies, commercial and open-source LLMs are evaluated against recent Pew Research Centre surveys. Study 1 shows that GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 can approximate national-level response distributions more accurately than uniform, normal-distribution, and historical-average baselines, with GPT-4 achieving mean absolute errors of approximately 4–8.5%. However, the models also exhibit important threats to validity, including underrepresentation of Republican viewpoints, underestimation of uncertainty, and, in some cases, overly homogeneous response distributions. Study 2 extends the analysis to GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, and Llama 3.3, showing that aggregate predictive accuracy generalises across models but that partisan alignment and distributional fidelity are model- and topic-dependent. Study 3 demonstrates that collective-level estimation is more valid than aggregating persona-based individual simulations, which produce substantially higher error and stronger homogeneity bias. Ablation tests further indicate that predictions are relatively robust to role prompts and temperature settings but sensitive to survey-item context. These findings suggest that LLMs may be useful as exploratory and supplementary tools in public-opinion research. However, the responsible use of LLMs requires explicit validation against human data, attention to bias and uncertainty, and careful integration with established principles of survey design.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Analog circuit design automation requires both coordinated tool execution and efficient numerical search. Large language models (LLMs) offer new ways to organize tool execution, but finding one sizing that satisfies specifications across process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners remains costly. PVTSizing 2.0 addresses these needs through a human-agent workflow built around an independently usable numerical optimizer. An agent carries the designer's approved task through execution and result review. The optimizer reduces unnecessary training through loss-guided updates and uses critic-guided local refinement to explore additional candidates while accounting for cross-corner conflicts. An optional LLM adviser supplies parameter relationships to focus numerical search on circuit-informed directions, while the optimizer selects adjustment amplitudes and verifies their effects through simulation. Across four circuit benchmarks, the standalone optimizer completes all 40 runs and achieves a 7.3x speedup in overall mean runtime over the original PVTSizing, with a comparable mean sample count. In a separate study, the best tested knowledge-injection configuration further reduces mean runtime by 39.9% and simulation samples by 35.4% relative to the standalone optimizer.

While education shifts further into the digital age, human connection remains irreplaceable. Effective learning is fundamentally a deeply social process, where robust relationships with peers, educators, and communities are indispensable to cognitive, emotional, and ethical development (Noddings, 2013; Vygotsky, 1978). As higher education is increasingly shaped by advanced digital technologies including Generative AI and AI-enabled learning systems, it is essential that educational innovation moves beyond technological capability to consider how advanced technologies can foster human connection, cultivate belonging, support collaboration, and enhance individual and collective wellbeing (Holmes et al., 2019; UNESCO, 2023). This view aligns well with Fink’s (2013) taxonomy of significant learning, which recognises that understanding oneself and others (the human dimension) is a critical component of learning, an integrated process comprising six interrelated dimensions. Cultivating this dimension is vital for developing new values and interests that sustain life-wide and life-long learning, and advance learners’ academic and personal development. With life-wide and life-long learning in mind, we extend Chen’s (2025) learning taxonomy approach that is grounded in Bloom’s (1956) and Fink’s (2013) learning taxonomies to adopt a sociotechnical approach to the design of a postgraduate Information Systems (IS) unit. We designed learning activities and assessments that not only develop disciplinary knowledge and skills required to achieve unit learning outcomes but also empower students to cultivate new values and interests that sustain life-wide and life-long learning. Student feedback and reflection have been positive, suggesting that this approach fosters deep engagement, enhances meaningful learning and increases students’ metacognitive development. We will share key reflections from our teaching practice and invite discussion to explore how sociotechnical approaches can inform the design of AI-enabled IS education to advance life-wide and life-long learning.

As higher education institutions accelerate the adoption of generative AI, questions of trust, human agency, and educational purpose are becoming central to the future of technology mediated education. This paper argues that AI has not created a crisis in higher education so much as exposed and accelerated declining trust within teaching, learning, and assessment. Drawing on Humboldt’s conception of the university as a site of productive living tensions, this disciplined provocation examines how technology-mediated education is reshaping the relationships between learners, educators, knowledge, and algorithms. Drawing on inductive theory generated from a two-year constructivist grounded theory study, this paper proposes the notion of epistemic crisis as a way to represent the deficit dialogue driving epistemic change, and the concept of generative distrust exposing the fractures between the productive living tensions that build trust in higher education. The paper contributes to contemporary debates on human-centred learning design by arguing for a rebalancing of the algorithm through pedagogies that foreground care, collegiality, civic engagement, controlled risk and collective mission.

Medical imaging is a cornerstone of modern healthcare, driving advancements in diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient care. Among its various tasks, segmentation remains one of the most challenging problems due to factors such as data accessibility, annotation complexity, structural variability, variation in medical imaging modalities, and privacy constraints. Despite recent progress, achieving robust generalization and domain adaptation remains a significant hurdle, particularly given the resource-intensive nature of some proposed models and their reliance on domain expertise. This survey explores cutting-edge advancements in medical image segmentation, focusing on methodologies such as Generative AI, Few-Shot Learning, Foundation Models, and Universal Models. These approaches offer promising solutions to longstanding challenges. We provide a comprehensive overview of the theoretical foundations, state-of-the-art techniques, and recent applications of these methods. Finally, we discuss inherent limitations, unresolved issues, and future research directions aimed at enhancing the practicality and accessibility of segmentation models in medical imaging. We maintain a GitHub Repository to continue tracking and updating innovations in this field.

Background : LLMs increasingly draft personalized academic outreach, which depends on describing a real professor's research. Unsupported claims about a recipient's topics, methods, or findings misrepresent their scholarly work. Methods : In an offline pilot, a 2 × 2 design varied whether the writer received a publication evidence packet during drafting and whether a verifier revised the draft afterwards (conditions A–D). We generated 96 emails for 12 professors across three fields, decomposed them into 360 atomic research claims, and labelled each against the professor's evidence packet with an automatic (LLM) evaluator. All primary estimates are pilot estimates from automatic labels, not human-verified measurements. Reliability was assessed against a blinded 36-claim human-labeled subset (10% of claims) and a second automatic evaluator from a third model family. Results : Under the primary evaluator, the closed-book baseline (A) had a Severe Error Rate (SER) of 0.344 (21/61 claims; exact 95% CI 0.227–0.477). Grounding the writer (B) produced no severe errors in 90 judged claims (0.000, CI 0.000–0.040) and raised Supported Personalization Density (SPD) from 0.65 to 1.71 supported claims per 100 words. Verify-only (C) left 1 severe error in 50 claims (0.020; SPD 1.04); grounded-plus-verified (D) produced none (0/87) at the highest specificity (1.76). Interpretation and limits: Primary-evaluator agreement with the human annotator was only fair (Cohen’s κ = 0.33, CI 0.16–0.49). The evaluator was too lenient in 14 of 16 disagreements, suggesting that the automatic severe-error rates may underestimate error prevalence. However, the small human-labelled subset does not establish the magnitude or direction of bias across the complete dataset. The zeros are evaluator-specific: a second evaluator relabelling the same claims found 10 severe errors in B and 4 in D, closed-book 0.455 - a large reduction under grounding, not elimination. And 17 of the 21 closed-book severe errors came from the four psychology professors; excluding that field, closed-book SER falls to 0.095. Both automatic evaluators reported lower pooled severe-error rates for grounded conditions than for ungrounded conditions. Grounding during drafting also showed a lower observed pooled SER than post-generation verification alone. Conclusion : Verified publication evidence sharply reduced severe misrepresentation - to zero under the primary evaluator, roughly four-fold under the second - while making emails more specific, and outperformed correcting drafts afterwards. Grounding, not correction alone, is the more promising safeguard; establishing the effect size needs human labelling at scale and a validated judge.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The past two decades have seen higher education progressively rely on digital-enabled teaching and learning systems. Learning management systems, lecture recordings, online readings, assessment technologies, and increasingly flexible modes of participation have transformed the student experience (The University of Queensland, 2021, 2025, 2026a, 2026b). In this context, digital technologies have become an essential and expected component of contemporary higher education (The University of Queensland, 2021, 2026a). This Pecha Kucha explores how the rapid evolution of educational technology, culminating with the emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), is prompting educators and students to reconsider questions of authenticity, trust, creativity, and what makes learning memorable, meaningful and distinctly human (Lao et al., 2026; Polyportis, 2023; Rajan & Niranjan, 2025). As GenAI becomes embedded in education, learners are increasingly navigating blurred boundaries between real and generated experiences (Çalli & Alma Çalli, 2025; Lao et al., 2026; Weikmann et al., 2025). Content that once inspired fascination, curiosity, or wonder is increasingly met with scepticism (Çalli & Alma Çalli, 2025; Weikmann et al., 2025). This raises questions about what forms of learning remain uniquely valuable when information, content creation and digital assistance are readily available (Polyportis, 2023; Rajan & Niranjan, 2025). The challenge facing higher education is not whether technology belongs in learning environments, but how it can be meaningfully used to engage students in the learning process. Two examples illustrate this approach. In a humanities literature course, students engaged with the University of Queensland library collections and spaces before developing creative responses to course texts through zines, journals or rewritten scenes. Students could work in paper-based or digital formats, supporting creativity, personal expression and engagement with disciplinary ideas. The resulting exhibition demonstrated diverse interpretations of course concepts and encouraged ownership of learning. In an archaeology course, Gradescope was used to support assessment and feedback processes while learning remained centred on collaborative, in-person activities, creating a tangible “mycelium web” of theory, mapping relationships between concepts into a shared physical artefact. This approach supported collaboration, deeper conceptual understanding and the practical application of theory through active participation. In both examples, technology played a supporting role, enabling greater focus on curiosity, creativity, connection and meaningful learning experiences. While digital technologies have created opportunities for access, flexibility, and inclusion that were previously impossible, educators also have a responsibility to design learning experiences that cultivate curiosity, creativity, human connection, and shared discovery (Rajan & Niranjan, 2025; The University of Queensland, 2021, 2025, 2026a). Yet educators face challenges in selecting appropriate technologies, meeting assessment security requirements, and guiding students in the ethical use of GenAI and the development of human values (Al-Shamaileh et al., 2026; Qin et al., 2025; The University of Queensland, 2026b). Learning designers and other third-space professionals contribute expertise in bringing educators, technologies and human-centred pedagogies together to create engaging learning activities and assessment. Through these examples, attendees will be encouraged to consider how learning environments can foster connection, trust, and engagement in an increasingly AI-mediated world. They will gain practical insights into using technology strategically while preserving the human qualities of learning that foster curiosity, belonging, and participation.

This study examines how authenticity is constructed and reconfigured within deepfake generation and detection systems. Drawing on the perspective of Science and Technology Studies (STS) and the methodological framework of Critical Technical Practice (CTP), it conducts a critical analysis of the core code of two representative open-source projects, FaceFusion and DeepfakeBench. Through the syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic dimensions of code, the study investigates how authenticity judgments are technically operationalized within deepfake systems. The findings reveal three interrelated processes through which authenticity is reconfigured in deepfake technological systems. First, authenticity undergoes Proxyization, as direct judgment of authenticity itself is increasingly suspended and verisimilitude comes to function as its technological proxy. Second, authenticity undergoes Riskification, as authenticity judgment shifts from factual verification to risk calculation and risk balancing. Third, authenticity undergoes Residualization, as technological systems establish authenticity by continuously identifying and excluding falsity. Consequently, authenticity no longer functions as a positive category requiring direct confirmation. Instead, it becomes a negative category established through the negation of falsity and exists only as the residual state left after falsity has been continuously identified and excluded. More importantly, these processes demonstrate that deepfake technologies are driving a profound transformation of the digital information environment: credibility is increasingly established through the exclusion of falsity rather than the confirmation of truth, thereby reshaping the fundamental logic through which authenticity is established and trust is sustained within the broader social information environment.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Education-focused academics are important to learning and teaching in Australian higher education yet often face fragmented academic identities and uncertain promotion pathways within research-intensive cultures that reward research over educational expertise (Fleischner & Lutze-Mann, 2025). These challenges are often amplified for women across a range of academic and higher education career pathways, including roles spanning academic and professional domains. Education-focused expertise is frequently respected externally yet under-recognised within academics’ own institutions, compounding isolation and invisibility (Brown et al., 2024). This poster shares the collective reflections of education-focused women from Curtin University, The University of Queensland, The University of Sydney and The University of Western Australia, connected through the ASCILITE Women in Academic Leadership (WiAL) program. Established in 2021 to address women's underrepresentation in senior academic roles, WiAL operates as a cross-institutional community of practice built on structured mentoring, peer coaching, webinars and regular connection (Bone et al., 2024). Drawing on reflective narratives and examples, we explore how the WiAL community operated as collaborative professional learning, drawing strength from our diverse perspectives and perseverance through the inevitable tensions of education-focused work. With a shared interest in technology-enhanced learning, we make sense of our academic identities across markedly different institutional conditions for education-focused work. We outline how the community supported tangible career outcomes: preparing for and achieving promotion, pursuing learning and teaching grants, building publication momentum, and naming and disarming imposter syndrome. Connections forged through the network have already generated scholarly collaboration, including contributions to a cross-institutional edited collection on generative AI in learning and teaching (Fitzgerald, 2025; Vallis, 2025). Institutional evidence confirms that education-focused academics progress to the most senior levels when career development, connection and recognition are deliberately cultivated (Fleischner & Lutze-Mann, 2025). Mentoring structured across institutions and free of institutional hierarchies builds capability while countering the isolation experienced by women at the nexus of education and technology (Gribble et al., 2024). Our experiences affirm that such communities foster visibility, gravitas and relationships (Brown et al., 2024), enabling collective strength over individual competition. Sustained digitally across four states, our community models the conference theme: connection, collaboration and compassion enacted through technology. We share practical insights into reflective career communities that can build resilient and sustainable education-focused careers through meaningful, technology-mediated connection.

This paper reports initial findings on how the top 10 Australian universities have responded to Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) through their academic integrity policies, guidelines, and AI-related governance documents. Using qualitative policy analysis and thematic analysis of institutional policies and guidelines, this study examines how GenAI use is framed and governed, including how institutional expectations are communicated to students, academics, and administrators. The study also explores how universities frame the opportunities and risks associated with GenAI. The initial findings show a clear shift away from prohibition and surveillance-oriented approaches once common in higher education. Rather than relying on AI detection tools, universities are increasingly emphasising responsible use, transparency, assessment redesign, and shared accountability among students and educators. Academic integrity is being reframed as a matter of learning design and ethical participation rather than solely as compliance and enforcement, moving from a detective to an educative approach. These findings suggest that Australian universities are seeking to balance technological innovation with educational values, offering insights for institutions navigating the evolving relationship between GenAI, assessment, and learning. This paper contributes to ongoing discussions on how higher education can effectively integrate AI while fostering trust, safeguarding academic integrity, and enhancing meaningful learning.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Preparing, executing, and validating strongly coupled multi-physics simulations require expert time. Agentic workflows use large language models (LLMs) to coordinate them from natural-language descriptions, but reliability requires checks of physical consistency and fidelity to the problem description. Our agentic harness implements explicit task allocation: LLMs interpret user requests and simulator diagnostics, generate input components not covered by predefined construction rules, and propose repairs, while deterministic routines construct supported components and check inputs, edits, and results. We evaluate CO2-storage problems using the multi-physics simulator GEOS, from compositional flow to flow-poromechanics with frictional fault contact. In 80 attempts on two flow problems, grounding raises the proportion of structurally valid inputs from 5/20 to 20/20, but acceptance reaches 20/20 only with complete rule-based input preparation. With identical inputs, local repairs correct three seeded defects while preserving valid inputs. Supporting tests identify simulations passing physics checks despite differing from the problem description or reference results.

Amodal perception enables humans to perceive entire objects even when parts are occluded, a remarkable cognitive skill that artificial intelligence struggles to replicate. Recent diffusion-based methods have extended amodal completion from images to videos, yet they lack auxiliary priors to guide the reconstruction of heavily occluded content and to maintain temporal consistency over long sequences. We present REVEAL (REconstructing VidEo Amodal content via Language and flow guidance), a unified diffusion-based framework that integrates complementary motion and semantic priors for video amodal completion. A user-provided text query serves a dual role: it drives open-vocabulary video segmentation to obtain visible masks, and it provides semantic guidance for texture reconstruction. For amodal segmentation, we introduce optical flow guidance: by warping visible masks from previous frames to the current frame, the flow-warped mask propagates visible content into occluded regions and approximates the object's current shape, providing a strong shape prior even under simultaneous deformation and occlusion. For texture completion, text guidance constrains the reconstruction of occluded appearance while providing a stable semantic reference that helps maintain visual coherence throughout the reconstruction. We also contribute LAVAT, a new benchmark featuring long video sequences paired with text descriptions, enabling evaluation of text-guided video amodal completion under heavy occlusion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that REVEAL achieves state-of-the-art performance on existing benchmarks while maintaining high-quality temporal consistency over extended sequences. The project page is available at: https://uark-aicv.github.io/REVEAL/.

documents.abstract: The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has intensified discussions about assessment assurance, academic integrity, and graduate capability in higher education and vocational education and training (VET). Institutional responses have often prioritised assessment security, while a growing body of scholarship has sought to define the competencies required for AI literacy. This position paper argues that these developments, while important, risk overlooking longstanding educational traditions that remain highly relevant in AI-enabled learning environments. Drawing on critical literacy and Students-as-Partners scholarship, we contend that many capabilities now associated with AI literacy reflect enduring concerns regarding critical evaluation, ethical participation, and learner agency. Rather than proposing another AI-specific framework, we argue that established educational traditions provide a robust foundation for helping students engage with AI critically, ethically, and thoughtfully. We conclude by suggesting that educational responses to AI should prioritise critical dialogue and shared responsibility as students prepare for increasingly AI-enabled professional and social contexts.

Large-scale robotic simulation requires diverse deformable objects with executable physical properties and realistic interaction behaviors. However, existing 3D asset collections primarily emphasize visual diversity, while scalable physical construction and verification remain challenging. We introduce RFW-S, a large-scale dataset of 83,365 simulation-verified assets spanning 485 everyday categories across five structural families: soft solids, cloth sheets, shells, garments, and bags. We develop an automated pipeline integrating reference-guided 3D generation, structure-aware physical modeling, and LLM-assisted parameter estimation and calibration. To ensure physical reliability, we introduce an independent simulation verification framework that evaluates object behaviors under interactions distinct from those used for parameter calibration. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of independent verification and characterize deformable responses under different physical configurations. We further evaluate robotic grasping in terms of both task success and object integrity, and demonstrate the physical realism of our simulated objects through sim-to-real replay of fragile-object manipulation. RFW-S provides a scalable foundation for physically grounded simulation and embodied robotic learning.

Large language models (LLMs) have renewed interest in Page Stream Segmentation (PSS), splitting a multi-page file into its constituent documents. Yet published LLM methods still frame the task as boundary classification over one or a few neighboring pages, and commercial document-splitting APIs do not disclose their methods. We reimagine PSS for LLMs as a sequential process over the whole stream and propose RICoT (Recurrent Interleaved Chain-of-Thought), a prompting framework that works through the pages as a reader would: within a sliding window it reasons about each page and commits its boundary decision before moving on, and across windows it carries forward a compact record of what it has read, keeping per-call cost bounded. We also introduce FinancePSS-205, a benchmark of 205 real-world, de-identified financial page streams, to be released publicly. On FinancePSS-205, RICoT matches or outperforms pairwise and windowed prompting with the same backbone for each of three open-weight LLMs; on a TABME test subset, RICoT with GLM-5 reaches document F1 0.847 and boundary F1 0.915, above published zero-shot results. A 2B-parameter student, trained on a larger teacher's decisions with and without the page-level reasoning, performs comparably in both modes and comes within 0.05 document F1 of the strongest prompted model on FinancePSS-205.

A clinical AI system can reach a correct final diagnosis through intermediate decisions that could have harmed the patient, and can repair an error while introducing new risks. Most evaluations score final diagnoses; even stepwise benchmarks, which release a case's evidence over time, score whether systems reach the right diagnosis or gather the right information, not whether the decisions a patient passes through are safe. We make patient safety the target of stepwise evaluation. A trajectory audit replays real admissions checkpoint by checkpoint, lets each system decide with only the evidence released so far, and rates every test, treatment and disposition for its potential harm to the patient and, separately, for clinical validity, against the documented final diagnosis and physician-written disease rubrics yet on the evidence available when the decision was made. An LLM judge scores every decision, and a physician reference standard (triple annotation and senior adjudication of a stratified sample) calibrates the rates. An oversight audit branches each trajectory at its first actionable error and measures, on the same branches, whether corrective feedback repairs the error and whether it introduces new harm. Across 300 cases from a hospital cardiology cohort, MIMIC-IV and the public ASCENT benchmark, with up to seven AI systems per source, 55.2% of hospital trajectories reaching an acceptable final diagnosis passed through a decision with moderate or severe potential harm and 24.8% through a clinically unacceptable one; the harm rates were 76.2% on MIMIC-IV and 39.6% on ASCENT. Structured corrections resolved 73.6% of first errors versus 24.8% after bare rejection, yet new potentially unsafe decisions followed 30.2% of corrections versus 19.7% of rejections. A correct final diagnosis does not certify a safe trajectory, and a successful correction does not certify a safe recovery.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Teaching work is complex and multifaceted, involving demands that go beyond teaching and may favor occupational risks and mental health problems. This study aims to analyze scientific evidence on occupational risks and their repercussions on teachers’ mental health, characterizing the studies, describing their physical and psychological repercussions, verifying differences according to sex or gender, and analyzing coping, prevention, and intervention strategies. Methodologically, this is an integrative literature review, with a search in the Scopus database, from 2021 to 2026, in Portuguese and Spanish, which yielded 36 articles. Original full-text articles on basic education and/or higher education teachers were included, with data related to occupational risks or health problems. Quantitative, observational, and cross-sectional studies predominated. Thematic analysis organized the findings into risk factors, mental and physical repercussions, sociodemographic differences, and protective strategies. The main risk factors were work overload, role conflict and ambiguity, low autonomy, insufficient social support, technostress, work–family conflict, school violence, and career precariousness. The repercussions included burnout, Common Mental Disorders, anxiety, depression, insomnia, psychological distress, musculoskeletal pain, and vocal fatigue. Gender differences were observed, with greater female vulnerability due to the double workday, and variations according to educational level, with emphasis on academic productivism in higher education and postgraduate studies. Protective strategies combined individual resources, collective integrative practices, and institutional and ergonomic measures, although individual resources are insufficient without structural changes. Thus, teacher illness is multidetermined and articulates organizational demands, interpersonal relationships, and individual resources. Mental health promotion requires permanent institutional policies, reduced overload, social support, ergonomic adequacy, and spaces for listening. Finally, longitudinal studies and searches in multiple databases are recommended.

Background Female infertility often requires coordinated diagnostic, surgical, and assisted reproductive strategies. Robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) may facilitate selected fertility-preserving procedures, while artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to reproductive imaging, embryo assessment, ovarian stimulation, prognosis, and clinical decision support. The clinical evidence for both technologies is uneven, and direct AI integration into robotic infertility surgery remains early. Main body This critical review evaluates current evidence for RAS in myomectomy, tubal reanastomosis, endometriosis surgery, adhesiolysis, ovarian surgery, and selected reconstructive procedures, alongside clinically relevant AI applications in assisted reproduction and reproductive imaging. RAS may offer technical advantages in complex cases through enhanced visualization, instrument articulation, ergonomics, and suturing, but superiority over expert conventional laparoscopy for cumulative live birth, time to pregnancy, ovarian reserve preservation, and cost-effectiveness remains insufficiently established. AI can improve standardization and prediction, but many models remain retrospective, internally validated, incompletely calibrated, or insufficiently tested for clinical utility. We propose a clinical maturity framework that distinguishes current surgeon-controlled RAS from research-stage AI support and speculative autonomous surgery. The most plausible near-term AI-RAS integration is clinician-supervised support for preoperative imaging, surgical difficulty prediction, intraoperative video analytics, robotic skill assessment, postoperative fertility prognosis, and sequencing of surgery and assisted reproductive technology. Conclusion AI and RAS may become complementary components of female infertility care, but routine integrated use requires multicenter prospective validation, standardized infertility-specific outcomes, transparent AI reporting, patient-centered evaluation, regulatory oversight, and assessment of cost and equity.

In multi-agent systems, a receiver agent often waits for a helper agent's message (text or its latent KV cache), which can improve performance but adds latency. We study when a receiver agent can skip the message safely (the final answer rarely changes) and beneficially (the time saved exceeds the cost of deciding). Our mechanism reads the receiver agent's confidence without the message and uses a finite-sample test to certify a threshold at which, with high probability, at most 5% of skipped answers change; if none passes, the system keeps communicating. We test it on OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU-Pro with three Qwen model pairs, on cross-family agents, and on SQuAD and GSM8K. Four insights emerge. First, oracle headroom is weak evidence that messages help: control inputs without answer-specific content, matched to change answers as often as real messages, reproduce a median 76% of the oracle's gain. Second, whether a message can be skipped depends on how often and how predictably it alters the answer, not on its accuracy; every certified KV-cache path is less accurate than the receiver agent alone. Third, where text messages help, skipping keeps most of their gain: on unseen questions in the four such settings, the policies skip 59 to 80% and keep an estimated 76 to 95% of the gain. In two prospective tests with all rules fixed in advance, our mechanism skips a three-agent system's verifier on 39.9% of sealed questions, keeping 12.55 of its 12.80-point gain, and a 32B helper on 68.4% of held-out questions, keeping its whole gain. Fourth, safety does not determine efficiency: at batch size one, skipping text saves hundreds of milliseconds per query and skipping KV cache far less. Certification extends to SQuAD but not to GSM8K. In eleven tests on unseen questions, every certified policy we could test kept its change rate's 95% upper bound below 5% under our answer parsers.

The article analyzes the concept of resilient safety (Safety II) proposed by the Danish psychologist Erik Hollnagel, one of the leading specialists in the field of safety and reliability of sociotechnical systems. Despite the authority of this concept, the analysis shows that it has an almost …

Preference alignment has become a central tool to align large language models (LLMs) with human values and desired behavior, and its online variant can further advance their capabilities beyond what static data alone offer by repeatedly generating and labeling new responses with human feedback. But costly, time-consuming annotations limit its scalability, making sample efficiency essential, and existing methods typically seek to improve it by expanding coverage of the response space or selecting pairs with the highest uncertainty for comparison. Although they are effective, these methods quantify uncertainty from the perspective of the LLM, which may differ from the uncertainty perceived by the user: a pair can appear highly uncertain to the LLM even when past comparisons from the user already imply a clear ordering. In this paper, we propose multidimensional preference-guided online direct preference optimization (MPG-DPO), which leverages low-cost multidimensional evaluations from automated verifiers on the user historical comparisons to construct a personalized preference cone guiding response selection for online preference alignment. Specifically, it first discards responses that are confidently dominated under the estimated user preference, then selects two responses that are competitive under the retained preference cone yet exhibit the strongest unresolved disagreement. Theoretical analysis shows that, with high probability, the fraction of queries spent on cone-dominated responses vanishes as learning progresses. Experiments across multiple LLM families show that MPG-DPO outperforms strong contenders under matched query budgets.

Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as central foundation models combining multimodal perception with text comprehension. While VLMs are traditionally built via late fusion by continued pre-training an off-the-shelf language model on multimodal (image-text) data, mixing modalities from the start of pre-training (early fusion) has recently gained traction. However, the fundamental trade-offs between these paradigms remain poorly understood, resulting in expensive and heuristic-driven training recipes. In this paper, we systematically analyze the learning dynamics of these multimodal pre-training processes, showing that validation losses during vision-language fusion can be modeled by separating the base learning trajectory, where different data types contribute at distinct rates, from a distribution shift driven by the competition between modalities. We derive a scaling law that unifiedly describes these dynamics, enabling accurate loss predictions across mixture ratios, training steps, and model sizes. Crucially, our law characterizes the trade-off between early and late fusion: under a fixed data budget, early fusion preserves text performance while late fusion favors vision performance, yielding a trade-off that increasingly tilts toward early fusion as model size scales. Extensive experiments confirm that our scaling law reliably captures multimodal learning dynamics and governs fusion decisions.

Aim: Neoadjuvant therapy for locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) yields variable patient responses. Artificial intelligence (AI) and digital pathology offer a novel approach to preoperatively predict treatment outcomes using histomorphological features, potentially guiding organ-preserving strategies. This scoping review maps the current literature on AI-driven neoadjuvant response prediction in LARC to evaluate algorithmic performance and identify methodological gaps. Methods: Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines, a structured search of PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library was conducted for studies published within the last 10 years. Studies applying AI algorithms to pretreatment whole-slide images (WSIs) to predict neoadjuvant response in LARC were included. Results: Eleven publications were included. Ten studies used retrospective cohorts only, whereas one study also included a prospective validation cohort of 100 patients. Algorithmic frameworks predominantly featured classical machine learning, using software extraction of predefined features, and deep learning for autonomous pixel analysis. Across heterogeneous endpoints and cohorts, standalone classical machine-learning models reported external validation area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.811-0.908 (prospective: 0.733), a hybrid microenvironment model reported external AUCs of 0.643-0.656 (prospective: 0.630), and standalone deep-learning models reported an external AUC of 0.723 (internal: 0.710-0.81). Critical limitations across the field include heterogeneous clinical target endpoints, inconsistent baseline staging, and a reliance on “black box” algorithms lacking true biological explainability. Conclusion: AI-driven digital pathology demonstrates strong potential for predicting neoadjuvant treatment response in LARC. However, safe clinical implementation will require standardized endpoints, multimodal integration, and prospective multi-centre validation of algorithms anchored in verifiable tumour biology.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Safety benchmarks for computer-use agents (CUAs) place the harm either in the intent of the task or on a single screen: a malicious instruction, an injected command, a phishing page. An agent that checks the task and each screen in isolation can pass them, so they do not test whether it combines facts seen on different screens. Yet in delegated work, harm often arises exactly this way: a fact about a person on one screen, a fact about an item on another, and a legitimate task that binds them. We introduce SEAM (Safety Execution Across Multiple screens), a benchmark of such cross-screen compositional harm: 600 multi-step, cross-application OSWorld tasks in which the instruction and every single observation are benign and only their combination is harmful. Minimal-pair variants that differ in one place, scored from the server log rather than by an LLM judge, locate where an agent fails. General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents carry out the harm in up to 92% of runs, yet decline when the user states it in one sentence. Agents open the decisive pages, so exposure is not the primary bottleneck. Asked about those pages, they flag the harm, and with thinking they often write the conflict into their reasoning and confirm anyway. Safety recognition thus does not reliably translate into safe execution, and the translation depends on the information channel: the same warning stops agents far more often in the user's instruction than on screen. Proprietary models are markedly more cautious. We release SEAM with its generator and quality gates at https://yuxuan2003.github.io/SEAM/ .
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promise for clinical outcome prediction in the intensive care unit (ICU), but collaborative fine-tuning across hospitals is constrained by privacy and data-governance concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative training without exchanging raw data, but conventional parallel FL requires coordinated participation and centralized aggregation, which can be challenging when institutions differ in training availability. We develop and evaluate a novel framework called sequential federated fine-tuning (SFF) framework that enables efficient and privacy-aware collaborative clinical outcome prediction in ICUs across multiple hospitals. By transferring low-rank adapters sequentially from one hospital to the next, SFF supports asynchronous learning, allowing institutions to remain offline until their turn while another institution performs local training. Using 45,149 ICU stays from 27 hospitals in the eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD), we applied low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct and compared SFF with centralized fine-tuning, local fine-tuning, zero-shot prompting, and federated averaging (FedAvg) for in-hospital mortality and three-class length-of-stay (LoS) prediction. SFF achieved performance close to centralized fine-tuning while outperforming local training and FedAvg. For mortality prediction, SFF reached AUROCs of 86.08% and 89.24% for Qwen-2.5-7B and LLaMA-3.1-8B, respectively; for LoS classification, it reached 75.32% and 76.57%. The advantage over FedAvg was observed across most hospital cohorts and remained evident when local training data were limited. Our work advances the practical, privacy-aware deployment of LLMs in multi-institutional clinical settings for collaborative clinical outcome prediction in ICUs.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Skills-based organizing replaces jobs and credentials with information on skills, which artificial intelligence now extracts from job postings, résumés and human resource records at scale. Whether this information is valid for the decisions it supports depends on whether research on skills intelligence and research on human resource management inform each other. We mapped 3649 documents published between 2000 and 2026, screened with a large language model audited against a human reviewer, using co-citation, bibliographic coupling and permutation benchmarks. Managerial and computational research form separate communities: only 13% of coupling links connect them, against 46% expected by chance, and the divide is sharpest between studies of the same practice, recruitment and selection. Computational research, 71% of output in 2023–2025, is itself split between recruitment technology and labor-market analytics; it validates skill information mainly against annotated text, about one study in seven relates it to outcomes, and almost none evaluate the decisions it informs. Taxonomies such as ESCO and O*NET do not bridge the communities; work analysis is the main bridge. We propose a skills intelligence value chain from data to outcomes, with five testable propositions, an audit protocol that translates regulatory requirements into validity evidence for each link, a data schema and mixed-methods design that integrate natural language processing with work analysis, and a research agenda for validating AI-produced skill information.
