documents.abstract: This study developed and evaluated a Smart Fume Detection, Extraction, and Filtration System for CNC Laser Machines at Cebu Technological University–Argao Campus to improve airborne contaminant management during laser cutting and engraving. Anchored in the Cyber-Physical Machine Tool framework, sensor-based monitoring, airflow and filtration principles, Sustainable Manufacturing, and Garvin's Eight Dimensions of Quality, the study employed a developmental research design. The prototype integrated MQ-4 and MQ-135 sensors, microcontroller-based control, automated ventilation, warning mechanisms, digital monitoring, and multistage filtration. Data were collected through 20 controlled operational trials involving plywood and acrylic specimens, technical measurement instruments, observation logs, and questionnaire evaluations from 100 purposively selected respondents. Descriptive statistics and inferential tests assessed technical performance, material-based differences, and contaminant reduction. Results demonstrated 91.7% detection accuracy, 91.2% sensor reliability, a 4.28-second response time, 53.9 CFM extraction airflow, and 77.4% filtration efficiency, meeting all established benchmarks. Mean measured fume concentration decreased significantly from 393.29 ppm to 88.97 ppm, representing a 77.38% reduction (p < 0.0001). Significant differences between plywood and acrylic were observed in detection accuracy, response time, airflow, and fume concentrations, but not in sensor reliability or filtration efficiency. The prototype obtained an overall quality rating of 3.82, interpreted as Reliable. Further sensor calibration, extended testing, and contaminant-specific occupational safety validation are recommended. The study supports Sustainable Development Goals 3, 4, 8, 9, and 12 through occupational health, technical education, safer working conditions, industrial innovation, and responsible production. Its sustainability contribution includes improved fume management, adaptable automation, and institutional operating and maintenance guidance, subject to further validation before broader implementation.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is changing how students learn and how they seek support. This conceptual paper develops social displacement theory to explain how GenAI may replace interpersonal encounters that would otherwise contribute to social learning, belonging, and access to future support. It proposes the ABCs of Human-GenAI Support Decision-Making, in which (A) achievement, (B) burdens, and (C) connections shape whether students rely on independent effort, human support, GenAI, or a combination of these resources. It then advances relational andragogy as an institutional response suited to connected adult learning in a digital society. Relational andragogy intentionally cultivates trust, compassion, mattering, psychological safety, and mutuality while preserving learner agency. Through these relational conditions, institutions can support achievement over time, respond compassionately to external burdens, strengthen students’ anchors of connection, and develop more informed human-GenAI support choices. The framework does not assume that human support is always preferable or that GenAI use is inherently harmful. Instead, we distinguish augmentative uses that expand access or prepare students for human interaction from substitutive patterns that may progressively weaken learning communities. Practical and theoretical implications are offered for educators, student support services, institutional policy, and future empirical testing.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in software development raises a knowledge-continuity question: how can organizations retain the human competences needed to evaluate, diagnose, and correct software as production is increasingly delegated? This theory-synthesis article connects research on production and evaluation expertise, practice-dependent competence maintenance, and software-process selection. Two literature-grounded conditional propositions identify residual organizational capabilities (P1) and the conditions supporting their continuity over time (P2). Their combined implications are examined through matched Waterfall and Scrum configurations. Prior studies explain when evaluation depends on production, how expertise may deteriorate, and how methods are selected; they do not by themselves determine when a competence-maintenance deficit is imposed by formal process commitments rather than adjustable work arrangements. The synthesis yields a conditional attribution criterion: a limitation can be assigned to the method only if feasible alternatives within that method cannot meet the same requirements under matched constraints. The constructed comparison establishes this distinction, not observed long-term competence retention. Supplementary File S1 provides a five-step managerial decision guide and two worksheets.

Writing is central to how students develop and demonstrate communicative competence, yet that development is increasingly difficult to observe as GenAI enters the writing process. This paper establishes a pre-GenAI stylistic baseline of student academic writing and characterises how unedited GenAI responses to the same assessment prompts differ from it. Using stylometric and writing analytics techniques, we analysed over 118,000 words collected in 2021 from 18 higher education students in a software engineering subject. Study 1 used the seven students who completed all four tasks to establish a within-cohort reference: the size and direction of stylistic change in the same students’ writing across two semesters and two rhetorical genres. Study 2 paired each of 59 authentic submissions with a length-matched, zero-shot response to the identical prompt from three large language models. Student writing moved toward shorter words, fewer rare terms and markedly higher readability. Unedited model outputs moved in the opposite direction on each measure, gaining lexical sophistication through a narrower working vocabulary at substantial cost to readability; the human–GenAI gap in readability exceeded the students’ own shift between semesters.

As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) advance toward understanding and interacting with the physical world, spatial reasoning becomes essential for understanding scene structure and anticipating the effects of physical changes. Existing spatial benchmarks have made substantial progress in evaluating spatial relations, memory, and viewpoint reasoning, but less systematically assess how models connect physical scene conditions with visual observations. We introduce SpatialCast, a benchmark that uses cast shadows to evaluate this ability. Cast shadows provide observable evidence of a 3D scene. Their image appearance depends on object geometry and pose, illumination, and viewpoint. We examine this relationship through three complementary tasks that assess scene-projection consistency, predict intervention-induced changes, and infer the physical changes behind visual transitions. The benchmark contains 21,000 synthetic questions with separate scene and geometry test partitions, complemented by 200 SpatialCast-Real questions from 20 photographed scenes. Evaluations show that closed-source MLLMs outperform general-purpose open-weight MLLMs and MLLMs designed for spatial reasoning, which remain near chance on the synthetic benchmark, while even strong closed-source models struggle with shadow-length and light-height judgments. We also use SpatialCast training data for GRPO post-training, improving open-weight MLLM performance on the benchmark. Further evaluations show improvements on several external spatial benchmarks, suggesting transfer of the learned capabilities. These experiments support SpatialCast as a controlled resource for diagnosing spatial reasoning capabilities and studying their learning and generalization.

Real-time streaming joint audio-video generation for character animation requires a generator to speak the requested transcript, maintain visual identity across chunks, and run within a strict playback budget. These requirements are difficult to satisfy simultaneously: chunk-wise autoregressive generation can accumulate transcript-audio misalignment and visual drift, while the few-step distillation needed for low latency often degrades spatial diversity and temporal quality. We present StreamChar, a streaming framework that separates long-horizon orchestration from short-window audio-video denoising. An LLM-based orchestrator uses the transcript and historical context to produce frame-aligned audio conditions, and a joint audio-video DiT performs local bidirectional denoising with reference and motion-frame conditioning. For efficient deployment, we use a two-stage distillation pipeline that first compresses the sampler and then fine-tunes the student under online chunk rollouts. A progress-aware pointer aligns partial transcripts with generated audio during rollout training, and a sink-chunk memory provides a persistent visual anchor for reducing long-horizon drift. Experiments on short-clip and long-horizon protocols show that StreamChar runs in real time on a single H100 GPU and provides a favorable system-level trade-off among transcript fidelity, audio-visual synchronization, visual quality, and streaming stability compared with recent joint and audio-driven baselines.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is now a common feature of many students’ study practices, and universities are grappling with its implications for assurance of learning, assessment, academic integrity, effective teaching, student support, and policy. Yet institutional responses are still often shaped by assumptions about student use, capability, trust, integrity, and learning (e.g., Bearman & Fawns, 2024). This project is part of the overall Student Perspectives on AI in Higher Education Project, a four-university collaboration investigating how higher education students in Australia understand and use GenAI in relation to themselves as learners. It included two large scale surveys in 2024 (Chung et al., 2024) and 2026. The 2024 phase of the project showed that GenAI had already become embedded in students’ academic practices, with over 80% of surveyed students in four Australian universities having used it for study-related tasks and nearly half using it regularly (Chung et al., 2026). However, the findings also revealed complex patterns of trust, usefulness, self-directed learning, equity, academic integrity, and pragmatic, task-specific engagement. While this 2024 survey provided an initial snapshot of student engagement with GenAI, the rapid pace of technological and institutional change necessitated a follow-up survey in 2026 for an updated understanding of student practices and experiences. The 2026 survey was adapted from the 2024 instrument and comprised 50 questions and 115 items across demographics, use and usefulness, motivations, assessment and academic integrity, learning and fluency, and perceived impact (Henderson et al., 2026). The survey received 10,222 student responses, with 8,700 students fully completing the survey. The sample included 73% undergraduate students, 75% students aged 18 to 24, 59% women, 29% students who spoke a language other than English at home, 19% first-in-family students, and 24% students who identified as having a disability, health condition, or as neurodivergent. This Pecha Kucha presents descriptive findings from the 2026 survey and, where appropriate, compares these with findings from 2024. The recent 2026 data suggest that student use of AI for study has become more frequent: 20% of students reported daily use and 35% weekly use, compared with 13% daily and 31% weekly in 2024. The most common uses include editing or improving writing, generating ideas or examples, teaching students how to do something, finding information or conducting research, and getting feedback on work. Further, the presentation explores new areas of inquiry introduced in 2026, including AI summarisation of course materials, motivations for using or limiting AI, and AI fluency and learning. Among students who used AI for study, the strongest reasons for use were that it made things faster, helped them get unstuck, made things easier, reduced stress, and increased confidence. The strongest reasons for limiting or avoiding AI included concerns about inaccuracy, personal learning values, wanting to do the work themselves, worry about breaking rules, and ethical concerns. By presenting emerging 2026 findings alongside selected 2024 comparisons, this presentation argues that student voices are essential to developing sustainable, ethical, and educationally meaningful institutional responses to AI in higher education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Logical reasoning is a highly valued capability in language models. However, high-quality logical reasoning data remain scarce, while manual data creation is costly and time-consuming. We introduce Operations Research Aided Synthesis (ORAS), a solver-verified, two-layer incremental framework for synthesizing logic question-answering data. ORAS leverages operations research techniques to systematically generate high-quality datasets for evaluating large language models (LLMs) and, when used for training, improving their reasoning capabilities. ORAS’s pipeline integrates mathematical programming methods to generate question–answer pairs, and then employs a dual-phase approach: the first phase uses optimization algorithms to construct and evaluate the logic systems by solving the problem using a mathematical solver. The second phase translates the logic system to human-readable problems and generates answers according to the information from the mathematical solver. The fine-tuned model achieves a 22–33% (percentage point) improvement in accuracy on in-sample tests and a 4–22% (percentage point) improvement on similar out-of-sample tests.

Background: The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has dramatically advanced the capabilities of Natural Language Processing (NLP), enabling breakthroughs in text understanding, generation, and reasoning. However, the success of these models hinges on access to massive, diverse, and high-quality labeled datasets. In many real-world scenarios, such as specialized domains (e.g., healthcare, law), low-resource languages, and privacy-sensitive applications, curating such data remains prohibitively expensive, time-consuming, or infeasible due to regulatory or ethical constraints. Moreover, as LLMs continue to scale in size and complexity, the demand for training and evaluation data grows disproportionately, exacerbating annotation bottlenecks and domain coverage gaps. Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) has emerged as a powerful paradigm to address these challenges by programmatically producing task-specific or domain-adapted examples that complement or replace manually labeled data. Initially grounded in statistical modeling and deep generative architectures, SDG has evolved into a central strategy for improving data efficiency, mitigating distributional shifts, and enabling scalable supervision in modern NLP pipelines, especially in conjunction with LLM-driven prompt-based learning and self-supervised generation. Objectives: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of SDG techniques up to November 2026, with a particular focus on LLM-oriented pipelines. We categorize generative approaches for synthetic text, identify trends in controllability, verification and automation, and highlight open challenges in evaluation, fairness, privacy and scalability. Methods: We review the model families used to generate synthetic text, including probabilistic models, autoencoders and variational autoencoders, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), transformers, diffusion language models and mixtures of experts, as background for LLM-based pipelines such as instruction synthesis, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), prompt evolution, feedback loops and multi-agent generation, together with toolkits such as PromptSource [1], Self-Instruct [2] and LM-Debugger [3]. The original literature was collected informally; we extended it with a documented search run on 14 November 2026 (49 queries, 78 candidate records, 47 works added) covering 2025–2026 work on reasoning traces and verifiable rewards, model collapse and data quality, agentic and multi-agent pipelines, and evaluation, privacy and multilingual generation. The scope is text and language data, with other data types only where an LLM generates or directs their generation, and every reference was checked against arXiv, Crossref or the publisher. Results: Our synthesis traces an evolution from static, single-model pipelines to modular, verifier-centred and agentic systems in which LLMs plan, generate, critique and check data. Since 2025, synthetic data has become central to teaching models to reason: verifiable rewards move the bottleneck from preference labels to problems with checkable answers, which procedural generators, rephrased web text and self-play now supply. Studies of model collapse show that accumulating real and synthetic data avoids collapse while replacing real data does not, but also that even small synthetic fractions and recursive training can degrade models and their fairness. Synthetic text can leak membership information about its source data, and differentially private generation methods are narrowing the utility gap. Evaluation practice remains fragmented, and multilingual generation increasingly relies on culturally grounded rather than translated data. Conclusions: LLM-driven SDG is rapidly transforming data creation, making it more scalable, controllable and adaptive, but its reliability now depends on verification, provenance and privacy safeguards. This survey offers a taxonomy and a roadmap for building trustworthy synthetic data systems, and it motivates future work on verifiers beyond checkable domains, standardized evaluation of data generators, collapse-aware data practice and formal privacy guarantees.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping Design and Technology (D&T) education by transforming how design ideas are generated, evaluated, and refined. Although existing research has largely focused on capabilities and limitations of AI, less is known about the emerging teacher–GenAI relationships during authentic design practice. Through semi-structured and recall interviews, classroom observations, reflective journals, design folios and artefacts, this qualitative case study investigated these relationships. Guided by sociomaterial perspectives and using reflexive thematic analysis, the study examined how creativity, agency, knowledge construction, pedagogy, and ethical decision-making emerged through human–GenAI interaction. Findings revealed that pre-service teacher–GenAI partnerships evolved through a developmental trajectory from utility, to dialogue, to teacher orchestration, and ultimately allyship. Rather than functioning as a solution-generating tool, GenAI became a provocateur and generative partner whose educational value emerged through iterative cycles of prompting, critique, reflection, and redesign. The study proposes Orchestrated Co-Agency and the Teacher–GenAI Relationship Continuum as complementary conceptual lenses for understanding these interactions. These lenses could offer new theoretical insights into human–AI co-creation and inform curriculum, pedagogy, and the responsible integration of GenAI in Design and Technology education.

This Pecha Kucha presentation offers a situated account of teaching and assessing in the evolving context of generative AI-mediated higher education. It aims to open up space for contemplation and dialogue around the complexities of the current teaching and learning landscape, where students and educators alike are grappling with new norms, and much grace and understanding needs to be extended on both sides as each learns from, and with, the other how to better navigate the complex nuances and permutations of AI-mediated academic work. Drawing on experiences from a postgraduate academic writing course that I teach, I share a selection of pedagogical vignettes and provocations emerging from my marking of the end-of-semester reflection assignments for the course. This assignment, requiring students to highlight key insights gained from the course and to reflect on these with reference to course discussions and their own scholarly practices, is one that I have greatly enjoyed marking over the years. However, vastly different patterns of engagement have been emerging from the students in recent semesters, and it seems evident that the affordances of generative AI, in changing how students tackle academic assignments, are at the same time disrupting some of higher education’s long-held assumptions about what constitutes learning, writing, and ownership. The pedagogical encounters highlighted include: students asking my own course chatbot to reflect on the course for them, reflections being flagged by AI-detection software as being potentially entirely AI-generated, diverse understandings regarding what constitutes one’s “own work” where AI has been used to assist in the writing process, and students unquestioningly accepting AI’s reformulations as “better” than their own (even when they were not). Encountering these has caused frustration, but I also see in these examples deeper epistemological and pedagogical tensions. Literacy scholars, particularly those working within an “Academic Literacies” perspective (e.g. Jones et al., 1999; Lea & Street, 1998; Lillis, 2003), have long argued that reading and writing are “social practices.” They are, in other words, situated within, influencing and being influenced by, the social and cultural contexts in which they take place. The educational landscape of today, with its myriad AI-assisted possibilities, raises questions of whether, how, and to what extent, our conceptions about “learning,” “writing,” and “ownership” may need recalibration. In fact, scholars have begun to recognise that current writing practices resulting in hybrid texts co-constructed by humans and AI are making it difficult, if not impossible, to identify distinct boundaries between AI-generated output and a student’s own intellectual efforts (e.g. Eaton, 2023; Wu et al., 2026). Higher education is in a season where excitement, curiosity, and unease about generative AI’s impact on academic work and learning sit in tension. Even as one who has actively sought to engage students in discussions of how we can productively and legitimately use generative AI in our writing, I found myself having unexpected reactions (of relief) when I encountered assignments with linguistic infelicities of the sort that suggested their writers had not used generative AI. The way forward, this presentation suggests, requires an intentional commitment to prioritise pedagogical approaches that foreground human connection – both in terms of cultivating a renewed intellectual and emotional connection of students with their own work, and in terms of building connection between students and instructors through open dialogue and compassionate, nuanced approaches to teaching and assessing.

The arrival of capable generative AI (GenAI) tools has posed a genuine and largely unresolved challenge for summative assessment in higher education. When AI-generated submissions evade institutional detection 94% of the time and examination scores rise sharply without any change in teaching, the evidentiary basis of take-home and invigilated assessment is genuinely in question. This paper draws on two lines of work to argue that classroom-based gamified problem-based formative assessment (GPBFA) offers a more durable response than detection-focused approaches. The first line is an empirical study of saval.app, a GPBFA platform evaluated through Keller’s ARCS motivational model across a full university semester (pre n = 41, post n = 44). Results across all four ARCS dimensions were encouraging (all p < .0001; Cronbach’s alpha > .93; composite 81% positive response rate), with near-zero motivational decline across 12 weeks. The second line is a review of UNESCO’s 2024 AI Competency Frameworks for Teachers and Students, which we argue are philosophically and pedagogically aligned with classroom GPBFA in ways the existing literature has not yet made explicit. Taken together, we suggest that moving assessment into the classroom — where it is live, observed, and problem-centred — may address both the integrity challenge and the AI literacy imperative that UNESCO frameworks define.

Large language models are increasingly deployed at low precision, yet quantization can degrade their performance. We study how quantization interacts with decoding settings such as the sampling temperature and top-p by examining how it distorts the model's next-token probabilities. Measuring entropy during generation across deployed temperatures, we find that quantization warms the model on average, and that temperature matters much more for the performance of a quantized model than for its full-precision counterpart. Because quantization and temperature both shape the next-token distribution, we investigate how much the sampling settings can undo what quantization changes, through our method TempQuant, which learns the quantized model's temperature and top-p to bring its next-token probabilities closer to the full-precision model's. We learn these settings at two granularities. The first is a single global setting per requested temperature, which finds nearly the same temperatures that tuning on labeled answers would, without any labels. Model cards typically recommend sampling a quantized model with the same settings as its full-precision counterpart, while we find that different settings can substantially improve its accuracy. On 3-bit Qwen3-4B, for example, global TempQuant raises MATH accuracy from 34% under the configuration recommended for Qwen's quantized releases to 51%. The second sets the temperature and top-p for every token, motivated by our finding that tokens whose rankings flip under quantization tend to need warming, while tokens whose rankings are preserved tend to need cooling. When quantization degrades accuracy substantially, TempQuant recovers much of it, and when degradation is lighter, it still brings the quantized model's behavior closer to the full-precision model's.

This article examines the application of gamification in literature education as a means of increasing students' motivation and engagement. It analyses the theoretical foundations of gamification, including self-determination theory and game-based learning principles, and describes a quasi-experimental study in which game elements such as points, levels, badges, quests and narrative roles were integrated into literature lessons. The findings indicate that a carefully designed gamified environment strengthens intrinsic motivation, encourages regular reading, improves participation in discussions and deepens students' interpretation of literary texts.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

documents.abstract: Australian higher education has responded to generative artificial intelligence with an ambitious program of assessment reform. Structural approaches, most visibly the two-lane model, seek to sustain trust in degrees by securing some assessments while opening others to AI partnership. This conceptual paper argues that the reform consensus, now sharpened by sector attention to assurance of learning and adaptive capabilities, addresses validity more directly than formation. Assessment tasks are not only measurement occasions; they can also be sites of the cognitive work through which capability develops. Drawing on cognitive apprenticeship, desirable difficulties and cognitive offloading, the paper introduces the apprenticeship layer: the stratum of entry-level cognitive work through which expertise has historically been developed and renewed. As AI is increasingly used to perform parts of this work in workplaces and universities, institutions face a risk of certifying capabilities without reliably preserving the practice through which those capabilities are formed. The paper proposes three principles for formation-centred design: friction by design, process as both learning and evidence, and a care floor of guaranteed human attention. It concludes that valid judgement and capability formation are different questions that assessment can and should be designed to answer together.

Designing an undergraduate systems thinking course in 2023 took months. Workshops, whiteboards, an academic drafting offline, iteration, constructive alignment, compliance, and endless box-moving on a digital canvas. One decision shaped the course: the learning designer judged 10 assessment submission points across 12 weeks excessive and argued to reduce them. The academic, who had taught the discipline for years, refused. Systems thinking concepts interlock, and a student who has not grasped one cannot proceed. The checkpoints were not overload; they were scaffolding. The design bent to the discipline, and the disciplinary expert was right. Generative AI could now compress much of that. It can propose a structure, recommend staggered low-stakes checkpoints for interdependent concepts, and draft the content beneath them. It might well have reached that assessment design faster. Learning designers are tempted to insist something irreplaceable is lost. Much of it is not: a considerable portion of that time was drag, and automating drag is a good outcome. The argument here is not that slowness was valuable. What mattered was less visible. Working on unfamiliar material, the learning designer frequently does not understand the subject. This is usually treated as a limitation. It is better understood as an instrument. The designer is an authentic novice, and their confusion is diagnostic: when an explanation fails for them, it will fail for a student (Wieman, 2007). This is the logic of usability testing: a designer cannot test an interface they already know (Nielsen, 1993). A language model can usefully simulate a novice reader. What it cannot replace is genuine uncertainty: having absorbed the discipline, it fills gaps silently rather than experiencing them. But the instrument only works under a particular social condition. To say “I do not understand this” to an academic, repeatedly, about their own subject, requires standing, which no third space role description confers (Whitchurch, 2008). It is built through months of meetings, shared frustration, and accumulated trust, and it is what made the academic willing to re-explain rather than dismiss. The re-explanation is where the design insight came from. This is the uncomfortable possibility. The inefficiency was not valuable in itself, but the relationship formed inside it, and the relationship is the precondition for the human contribution. Compress the process into an afternoon and the drag disappears, along with the conditions in which trust is made. We have no way to tell which parts of a slow process were waste and which were connection. This Pecha Kucha presents a real course design, concedes what AI could do faster, and identifies what it cannot replace: genuine uncertainty, professional judgement, and trust. For institutions adopting AI-supported workflows, the practical implication is to protect time for co-design and explanation, treating relationship-building as work rather than overhead. It closes with a question beneath the debates about AI and the third space workforce (Bearman et al., 2023; Huijser et al., 2024): if the relationship was produced by the inefficiency we are now eliminating, can human-centred design survive its own optimisation?

Emotional experiences are fundamental inputs to human development, yet we know surprisingly little about their distribution in everyday life. Research typically characterizes children’s emotional environments using global reports or brief observations, obscuring the real-time contexts in which emotions arise. Here, we used artificial intelligence to automatically transcribe and annotate daylong audio recordings from three samples totaling N=159 families with children aged 5 months-8 years old (48.43% female). Our findings reveal the architecture of children’s everyday emotional environments: positive speech was concentrated during play and music, and 25% of speech segments conveyed frustration, concentrated during routine caregiving. Mothers’ mental health did not predict affective speech, but lower child effortful control predicted more frustration in our toddler sample. Frustration peaked in early toddlerhood, suggesting that children’s growing independence at this age may reorganize family emotional environments. Overall, emotional speech appears to emerge from everyday activity, with meaningful shifts across development.
topics: Child and Adolescent Psychosocial and Emotional Development

documents.abstract: Soil health is essential for sustainable agricultural development, and soil microorganisms play an indispensable role in maintaining and improving it. Soil microbial communities influence soil’s physical, chemical, and biological properties through multiple pathways, including promoting nutrient cycling, improving soil structure, decomposing pollutants, and providing biological control against pathogens and pests. This paper comprehensively reviews the complex relationships between soil microorganisms and soil health, focusing on the key mechanisms by which microbial communities contribute to soil health enhancement. It also analyzes the effects of environmental and human factors on microbial community structure and function. In addition, the study discusses the specific applications of soil microorganisms in agriculture, particularly in bioremediation, microbial fertilizers, and biocontrol agent development. This study aims to reveal how soil microorganisms impact soil health, assess their potential applications in agricultural management, and provide scientific support for sustainable agricultural development and soil resource conservation.

Learning design is increasingly central to higher education, yet practitioners continue to grapple with questions of identity, recognition and collective purpose. Building on previous ASCILITE conversations about professional standards for learning design, this working symposium builds upon previous symposia on this theme to move from questions about what learning designers do to what learning design stands for. Participants will be invited to co-author draft principles for a Learning Design Manifesto, articulating the values, commitments and purposes that should guide the field in a period shaped by generative AI, institutional reform, hybrid education and demands for scalability. Through short provocations based on existing research, guided group work and live synthesis, participants will develop, test and prioritise candidate principles.

This article examines the theoretical foundations of the impact of adaptive pedagogical design in blended learning on the motivation of higher education students. The relevance of this research stems from the digital transformation of higher education, the need to ensure the continuity and quality of the educational process under martial law, and the growing demand for personalised learning tailored to students’ individual abilities, cognitive interests and motivational characteristics. It is emphasised that the effectiveness of blended learning is determined not only by the use of digital platforms and electronic educational resources, but above all by a pedagogically sound combination of classroom and online interaction, flexibility in the organisation of learning activities, and the provision of adequate pedagogical support. The essence of adaptive pedagogical design is explored as a purposeful system for planning, organising and adjusting the educational process, taking into account the individual characteristics of learners. Based on self-determination theory, the importance of satisfying students’ basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence and social interaction in maintaining intrinsic motivation for learning is substantiated. The role of digital educational technologies, learning analytics, personalised feedback and interactive forms of pedagogical interaction in the implementation of an adaptive approach has been identified. The scientific novelty of the study lies in the theoretical justification and systematisation of the pedagogical conditions for implementing an adaptive pedagogical design for blended learning, aimed at maintaining the motivation of higher education students. It is concluded that the comprehensive implementation of the proposed pedagogical conditions creates the prerequisites for enhancing the motivational potential of blended learning and improving its alignment with the individual educational needs of higher education students.

Generative AI has pushed universities to review curriculum at pace and scale, raising urgent questions about assessment, academic integrity and graduate capability. At Monash University, the Programmatic Assessment and AI Review (PAAIR) project required faculties to examine assessment and AI integration at program level. This paper asks how educational designers can support teaching teams to make program-level curriculum decisions while AI practice, policy and disciplinary expectations are still unsettled. We use a practice-based reflective case study methodology across the faculties of Science, Arts and Information Technology. Data sources include workshop designs, curriculum artefacts, participant feedback, program mapping outputs and facilitator reflection. Our analysis examines how Kaospilot methods, including vision backcasting, shared canvases and visible artefacts, created structured conditions for teaching teams to work with uncertainty, surface disciplinary values and make program-scale thinking visible. The cases show both the promise and constraint of adapting Kaospilot methods to faculty-wide change. The method helped create the human conditions for programmatic AI review, but its impact depended on artefacts, documentation, leadership, governance pathways and continuing educational design work. The paper argues that AI curriculum review requires structured social conditions to enact policy settings.

Many LLM benchmarks for languages other than English are translated, multiple-choice, or difficult to score automatically. We introduce The Shared Word (TSW-NL), a Dutch benchmark built around four core principles: it is language-specific, open-vocabulary, human-curated, and deterministically scored. Each puzzle gives three clues that describe different senses or uses of the same Dutch word. The clues are individually ambiguous, requiring the solver to combine evidence across multiple clues. We construct the benchmark from Dutch Wikipedia disambiguation pages, followed by automatic filtering and extensive manual curation. The final dataset contains 222 instances, with three independent human answers per test item. The task is clearly challenging: scores in our human study range from 49.5% to 61.0% and the highest-scoring open-weight model we tested reaches only 39.3%. Many others even score below 20%. At the same time, closed-source models show great progress: GPT-4.1 (April 2025) scores 59.2%, whereas GPT-5.6 Sol with max reasoning scores 88.8%. We believe this task provides a useful addition to Dutch model evaluation, plus a clear recipe that can be applied to construct a similar benchmark for other languages.

Maintaining academic integrity is a serious issue in higher education, affecting the paradigms governing the production and dissemination of human knowledge. Although a significant body of research has explored the ethics of AI tool usage in higher education settings, these studies have neglected to examine the power relations inherent within them. In response to this issue, this study employs Bourdieu’s theories of symbolic violence and actor-network theory to review the AI usage policies of Australian higher education institutions and mainstream academic journal publishers. Specifically, actor-network theory is first applied to identify the governance networks surrounding AI usage within the technological adoption process, thereby establishing that AI tools act as mediating agents that actively facilitate communication between institutions and users. Furthermore, symbolic violence provides a comprehensive explanation of the means by which power-holding institutions legitimise such governance. In summary, the aim of this inquiry is to expose and challenge the “false pretences” of AI ethics regulations that merely adjust, reinforce and gloss over the status quo, thereby channelling the potential of AI towards justice and combating latent human bias. documents.abstract: Calibrated trust is considered an important factor for human-system interaction in decision-making. However, definitions of calibrated trust are heterogeneous and research often lacks conceptual clarity. In our work, we conducted a theoretical integration to summarize approaches defining and operationalizing calibrated trust in automation and AI. We then mapped these approaches onto the trust development process that builds on the Trustworthiness Assessment Model (Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025) and the Organizational Trust Model (Mayer et al., 1995). The resulting Trust Calibration Points Framework (TCa-P) offers theoretical clarity and actionable insights for improving trust calibration by identifying six calibration points that can be calibrated to optimize joint human-system performance, and, as a consequence, effective human oversight: maximum joint performance benchmarking, trustworthiness assessment, alignment of individual standards, risk-benefit assessment, dispositions, and behavioral adaptation. The TCa-P emphasizes that trust calibration is not monolithic but instead happens at different points along the trust development process.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: As data systems increasingly support autonomous LLM-powered agents alongside human analysts, they require richer semantic infrastructure bridging analytical concepts and analytical operations. Existing metadata systems expose schemas, catalogs, lineage, and governance information, but provide limited support for representing operational semantics. We propose the Value Semantics Layer (VSL), an architectural abstraction that externalizes value semantics as persistent, planner-visible infrastructure. VSL introduces Value Semantic Types (VSTs), reusable operational semantic assertions capturing distributional, relational, process, quantitative, and policy-grounded semantics. Unlike descriptive metadata, VSTs enable planners to validate analytical operations, select appropriate operators, and guide analytical workflows. We present the motivation, formalization, architecture, and prototype realizations of VSL, and outline a research agenda toward AI-native semantic infrastructure for analytical systems.

Background Anxiety and depressive disorders affect over 500 million people globally, with a treatment gap exceeding 75% in low- and middle-income countries. Current diagnostic frameworks rely on clinical interview and self-report, with test–retest reliability of 0.20 to 0.67 for these disorders in DSM-5 field trials. Autonomic nervous system dysregulation is a well-established biological correlate of anxiety and depression. We report the first, to our knowledge, prospective clinical validation of an autonomic biomarker-based artificial intelligence system against a blinded psychiatrist reference standard in routine clinical practice. Methods We conducted a prospective, two-site diagnostic accuracy study at tertiary hospitals in Delhi and Kerala, India (CTRI/2023/07/054984). The Xaant Resting Autonomic Signature (X-RAS) platform, a three-layer LSTM with self-attention previously developed on an independent cohort of 2,349 participants and frozen prior to the trial, analysed electrodermal activity and blood volume pulse from 15-minute resting-state recordings and produced a four-class diagnostic classification. Of 180 participants enrolled, 170 completed the protocol. Out of these, 114 clinical participants with DSM-5 depression, anxiety, or comorbid disorders, and 56 reference group participants recruited from a long-term meditation practice tradition were considered. The reference standard was the DSM-5 diagnosis established by the site psychiatrist, who was blinded to the platform output. The primary outcome was Cohen's kappa for AI-psychiatrist diagnostic agreement within the clinical cohort. Results Within the clinical cohort, the platform achieved 93.0% agreement with clinical diagnosis (κ = 0.884, 95% CI 0.789 to 0.956), with 100% sensitivity for generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) detection in the GAD subgroup (n = 15, 95% CI 78.2 to 100). All eight classification disagreements fell along the depression–comorbid boundary, and the AI classification agreed with the patient's own self-categorisation in five of the eight. Performance was consistent across the two sites (Delhi 94.6%, Kerala 91.4%, p = 0.527) and across age, sex, and education subgroups. Classical autonomic markers separated the clinical and reference groups with moderate to large effect sizes (d = 0.53 to 0.84). Two of the physiological constructs of the development-cohort, namely Hypoactivity and Experience, were reproduced at the group level in independently diagnosed patients. A per-minute slope analysis of the tonic EDA signal showed a transdiagnostic reversal, where the baseline settled downward during rest in the reference group and drifted upward across all three clinical subgroups (Kruskal–Wallis p = 3.0 × 10⁻²²). Conclusions Resting-state autonomic AI analysis provides objective diagnostic support for anxiety and depressive disorders, with Cohen’s κ = 0.884 (95% CI 0.789 to 0.956) against psychiatrist-assigned DSM-5 diagnoses in routine outpatient practice. Direct comparison with published inter-rater or test-retest reliability estimates is not appropriate given differences in methodology and reference standards. The platform's low cost, portability, and suitability for non-specialist operators support scalability in resource-limited settings. External validation in primary care, community, telehealth, and non-Indian populations is the next step for the programme. documents.abstract: Think Before You Code (TBYC) is a benchmark pipeline for studying whether code-focused language models can reason about software issues in ways that resemble human engineering deliberation. The benchmark curates GitHub issue discussions into structured records, extracts human discussion artifacts such as problems, solutions, constraints, rationales, and trade-offs, and then prompts models to generate issue-level "thoughts" using retrieved code context and few-shot examples. It converts model responses back into the same artifact space and evaluates them against human annotations using complementary metrics for artifact type detection, metadata matching, tag overlap, and semantic summary similarity. Beyond scoring, this study includes visualization, leaderboard, and baseline tools that make it possible to compare models, prompting strategies, and extraction methods across repositories and issues. Think Before You Code is an end-to-end evaluation environment for measuring how closely LLM software reasoning aligns with human strategic judgment.

Graduates of vocational programmes in the new-generation information technology industry often match employers’ job requirements poorly, and the transition from classroom practice to real work remains difficult. In response to China’s national special training plan for field engineers, Xi’an Vocational and Technical College and Beijing New World Times Science and Technology Co., Ltd. established a joint field-engineer programme for Java development and technical support posts. This article presents a qualitative case study of that programme, based on documentary analysis of project records and institutional reports interpreted through research on workplace learning and boundary crossing. The programme rests on three supports (a substantive governance organisation, a digital industry-data platform and institutionalised standards), a five-part closed loop in which school and enterprise jointly select entrants, teach, build learning resources, manage the process and evaluate results, and a three-stage practical sequence that moves students from post recognition on campus, through project rotation in the enterprise, to certified post-holding. Reported outputs include donated training equipment, jointly developed digital teaching resources, competition awards and high first-destination employment, although these figures come from the programme’s own records and have not been independently verified. The analysis suggests that institutionalised rights and responsibilities, deliberate support for crossing the boundary between school and work, and continuous feedback from industry data are the features most likely to transfer to other colleges. Limitations and directions for outcome-focused research are discussed.

In June 2025 and February 2026, the wars involving the United States, Israel and Iran led to content about nuclear war being posted on social media, particularly on TikTok and Instagram. In this article, I ask what practices social media creators are enacting to deal with perceived nuclear danger and explore how the practices relate to the struggle for agency to participate in international politics. I utilised practice theory and digital ethnography to analyse 146 short videos, allowing me particularly to expand the relations of practice theory with visualities, the study of popular culture and world politics, sociotechnical imaginaries, and workshops as methodology. I find that practices that digital creators enact can be described as nuclear nihilism, postapocalyptic imagining, nuclear education, and social media self-reflection. While nuclear nihilism describes the tendency to approach nuclear danger with indifference rather than anxiety, postapocalyptic imaginaries are visual depictions of an often romanticised post–nuclear war landscape. Nuclear education aims to spread knowledge about nuclear weapons, and self-reflection about social media addresses the absurdity of producing videos on nuclear war at all. The role of agency is ambivalent: Whereas some creators expect to possess hegemonic agency in a postapocalyptic reality, others grieve about their missing agency regarding nuclear weapons politics and about changing life during a permacrisis at large.

We evaluated Jev, a non-generative decision model, for title and abstract screening using 4527 records from two systematic reviews of bipolar disorder treatments previously used in our 2024 Journal of Medical Internet Research study. Human decisions to retain records for full-text assessment served as the reference. In the primary analysis, Jev answered yes-or-no questions (Noul); at a prespecified 50% cutoff, sensitivity and specificity were 99.6% and 98.9% for light therapy and 93.2% and 93.5% for adjunctive pharmacotherapy. For direct model comparison, Jev used explicit include/exclude options (Choice) and the same prompts as GPT-5 mini and GPT-6 Astra. Jev Choice achieved sensitivity and specificity similar to or higher than those of GPT-5 mini and GPT-6 Astra, while API charges per 1000 records were US$0.043 for Jev, US$0.57 for GPT-5 mini, and US$7.39 for GPT-6 Astra. Jev retained all reports ultimately included in both reviews across all tested conditions and runs. Although these findings do not establish that decision models can replace human reviewers, they support Jev as a promising, low-cost alternative to the tested generative LLM configurations for assisting human title and abstract screening. Independent validation across diverse review topics is needed to assess Jev’s generalizability and utility in human-supervised screening workflows.

documents.abstract: The expansion of generative artificial intelligence makes it necessary to distinguish computational consumption, adoption, and problematic dependence. This article proposes Tokenaholics as an exploratory concept without diagnostic equivalence and combines an interdisciplinary critical review with secondary analysis of public aggregates from 2025 and 2026. It examines Anthropic usage profiles by country and occupational group, Vercel daily token and spending shares, and GitHub indicators. K-means using five variables selects a two-group partition among 121 countries, with limited separation (silhouette of 0.308). The GitHub– Anthropic comparison matches eight of the ten countries in the GitHub table. Computer and mathematical occupations have published shares of 23.80% in chat and 28.17% in the API in May 2026; these measures retain each channel’s denominator. Temporal evaluation of Ridge and three baselines does not support stable predictive superiority. Budget scenarios for 2027 combine token quantity and effective price under a constant mix. The findings describe geographic heterogeneity, differences between channels, and distinct distributions of tokens and expenditure. These results characterize the sociotechnical context without operationalizing or validating Tokenaholics, estimating the prevalence of dependence, or identifying causality. The contribution to computer science is to connect a bounded conceptual definition with reproducible analytical procedures and a future agenda for evaluating regulation, verification, and functional impairment.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background The Fishbowl is a discussion format: an inner ring discusses a prompt while an outer ring observes and swaps in (Bermudez, n.d.). When it runs well, the interaction reaches the interactive tier of Chi and Wylie’s (2014) ICAP framework, most strongly linked to deep learning. Novice teachers struggle to orchestrate so complex a discussion and often avoid it or run it as procedural theatre (Dillenbourg, 2002), while students lack the scaffolding to grasp what good discussion looks like or to notice their participation in real time. Fixed-seat rooms make the concentric-ring layout harder to set up. The shift An LMS-embedded learning tool can address these problems by scaffolding through the interface itself: built-in phase sequencing and role-specific views support teachers as drivers rather than executors (Dillenbourg, 2013), while giving students concrete moves for good discussion and cues to notice their participation. Such a tool was never technically impossible, only unjustifiable, requiring a software team and budget cycle for one learning activity. Generative AI now lets a single learning designer (LD) author and revise a version between deliveries, so refinement moves at the tempo of teaching rather than procurement. However, unmediated “vibe coding” is fragile across accessibility, security, and pedagogical validity. Vibe engineering (Willison, 2025) is the discipline that makes the speed safe. Development snapshot Vibe engineering can be brought to education by drawing on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) orchestration and collaboration-script theory (Fischer et al., 2013; Kollar et al., 2006): balancing under- and over-scripting (Dillenbourg, 2002), preserving intrinsic script constraints (Dillenbourg & Tchounikine, 2007), and scaffolding transactive discourse (Fischer et al., 2013). Each version is audited in a separate AI session against accessibility and security checklists, while pedagogical validity is judged by the LD through CSCL orchestration principles and classroom observation. Every update ships as one small static HTML file, stored centrally with no student data and no runtime AI, so it propagates automatically to every unit that uses it. Poster experience Live demonstration on two adjacent devices: the projected Fishbowl discussion phase (teacher-facing) alongside the private ideas phase (student-facing). Annotated walkthrough of core design elements with their theoretical warrants. A few major versions showing how the tool evolved, with a QR link to selected prompt history. The accessibility and security checklists, with a QR link to the open-source versions. Relevance to the theme: Human-centred learning design The Fishbowl builds connection through structured dialogue, and the tool preserves that priority. It orchestrates the room without mediating the conversation, and the interface directs student attention to peers rather than screens. The approach is not specific to one activity: in principle, any collaboration script an LD can specify pedagogically could be authored at teaching tempo (cf. Holstein et al., 2019). Next steps The tool will run across teaching periods in 2026, with observations of orchestration load, participation, and facilitator experience feeding back into design rationales, checklists, and successive versions. The two checklists will be released as open-source, citable Markdown artefacts for the LD community.

This exploratory study examines how collaboration structures and engagement processes are associated with interdisciplinary knowledge construction among pre-service professionals engaged in AI-focused instructional design. There is not enough empirical evidence about professional collaboration when designing AI-integrated supports for diverse learners (Martinez-Maldonado et al., 2021; Wan et al., 2021). Little is known about how participation structures relate to the depth of cognitive engagement and knowledge integration that emerges during that process. This study used an exploratory, process-oriented discourse analysis that combined qualitative turn-level coding with descriptive frequencies. The researchers analyzed video-recorded collaborative discourse among pre-service special education teachers and pre-service school psychologists (N = 14) from an interdisciplinary graduate seminar focused on AI-integrated instructional design. The analysis used turn-level coding of participation patterns, cognitive and metacognitive engagement, and activation of an expanded Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework. The expanded framework incorporates Psychological Knowledge (PsychK) and Interdisciplinary Knowledge (IK). The study examined 3111 analytic turns across three interdisciplinary groups. It explored how participation distribution and cross-disciplinary exchange related to epistemic depth during collaboration. Groups with more distributed participation and more cross-disciplinary interaction tended to engage more often in high-level cognitive and metacognitive processes. They also showed broader combined activation of PsychK and IK related to AI tool use, learner variability, and ethical considerations. Groups with more concentrated participation tended toward procedural or discipline-specific reasoning, with limited activation of PsychK and IK. These patterns suggest that collaboration structure may play a role in shaping the kinds of professional knowledge that become salient during AI-focused interdisciplinary work. The study involved three groups in one seminar, its patterns describe these groups and should not be generalized. Group composition by discipline is a plausible alternative explanation for some of them. This exploratory study conceptualized interdisciplinary collaboration as an epistemic practice. It offered empirical insight into how professional knowledge may be negotiated under conditions of AI-mediated educational change. It proposed the epistemic ceiling as an exploratory theoretical proposition for future testing. The findings have implications for interdisciplinary educator preparation programs that aim to support ethical and inclusive AI integration as a collective, relational process. Future research with larger and more diverse samples could examine whether these patterns generalize across institutional and professional contexts.

Women remain underrepresented in cybersecurity higher education and the workforce, with participation and retention influenced by confidence, belonging, professional identity, mentoring, and career readiness. While Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly supporting technical learning in cybersecurity, its potential to enhance students’ broader development remains underexplored. This conceptual position paper proposes a Human + Agentic AI mentoring ecosystem in which Agentic AI mentors complement, rather than replace, human mentors, educators, peers, and professional communities. Integrating Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT), women in cybersecurity literature, and human-centred AI design, we present a conceptual framework and design implications for Agentic AI mentoring that supports confidence, belonging, professional identity, career readiness and workforce transition. The framework extends AI beyond technical tutoring towards human-centred, co-designed mentoring across academic, social, and professional dimensions.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Audio-visual question answering on lightweight user devices requires balancing speed, memory usage, privacy, and communication. One approach is to run audio-visual encoders on a server and a lightweight language decoder on the user device, keeping questions local while offloading media encoding. However, transferring and processing the full multimodal representation remains costly. We propose a training-free, query-agnostic token pruning framework that constructs a compact, reusable memory before transmission. We define video spatio-temporal blocks and aligned audio windows as players and estimate their importance through Monte Carlo Shapley valuation. We use an embedding coverage objective that combines query-independent utility with cross-modal redundancy calibration and rewards unimodal diversity through marginal coverage gains. We retain the original token embeddings of high-scoring players under a limited token budget and transfer the resulting memory once for reuse across subsequent local questions. Experiments on Video-MME, Daily-Omni, and Video-Holmes using video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) and video-SALMONN 2 Pro (4B) show that our method achieves the best or tied-best QA accuracy among the compared compression methods across all evaluated settings. On Daily-Omni with video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) at 80\% pruning, our method improves accuracy by 12.86--14.62 percentage points over these methods while achieving the lowest device-side LLM prefill and decoding latency, with up to $1.92\times$ decoding speedup at comparable embedding memory usage.

The scientific article investigates the complex problem of the formation and dynamics of motivation in the educational and professional activity of university students within the framework of ongoing educational reforms. The study aims to determine the specific psychological and pedagogical features of students’ learning motives development and to substantiate a system of effective tools, conditions, and factors for increasing their cognitive and professional activity during their university studies. A complex of scientific methods was applied, including a systematic theoretical analysis of psychological literature and an empirical research project (surveying and diagnosing) involving approximately 300 1st, 2nd, and 4th-year students of Vinnytsia Mykhailo Kotsiubynskyi State Pedagogical University, alongside university professors. The findings revealed a highly contradictory dynamics of the motivational sphere across different years of study. While the majority of students maintain a responsible attitude toward their education, the direct cognitive interest, internal learning drive, and emotional satisfaction from the process significantly decrease from junior to senior courses. This drop in intrinsic motivation is gradually replaced by purely pragmatic and formal factors, such as the necessity of passing exams, external attendance control, and future career competitiveness. Based on the results, the key conditions for fostering sustainable intrinsic motivation were highlighted: ensuring intellectual independence, creating problem-based situations, offering a differentiated task system, encouraging freedom of choice, and implementing innovative teaching approaches. The practical value of the work lies in proposing over twenty specific interactive methods to enhance students’ motivational sphere through optimized teacher-student partnership.

Learning designers (LDs) play a critical role in supporting higher education teaching and learning, especially through periods of significant digital change, from the rapid transition to online learning during COVID-19 to the redesign of learning and assessment in response to generative AI. In this increasingly digital and AI-enabled higher education sector, learning design is inherently relational, requiring practitioners to meet academics where they are and support educational change through trust, collaboration and compassion. Yet much of this work remains hidden, and difficult to articulate and demonstrate using traditional institutional measures. While output metrics such as consultations, workshops and resources developed provide evidence of activity, they often fail to capture the relational, collaborative and transformative nature of LD practice. Drawing on King and Patterson’s (2026) conception of course design as an act of care, we argue that many of the most significant contributions of LDs are relational rather than transactional. To address this challenge Boreland et al. (2025) developed the Learning Design Evidence Framework (LDEF) which provides a structured approach to evidencing the relational work underpinning educational innovation. The framework makes visible how LDs build trust, foster collaboration, influence practice, and create the conditions for meaningful educational change using seven segments; Student-Centered Design, Curriculum Design and Innovation, Professional Development, Promotion and Sharing of Quality Design, Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, Leadership and Influence, and Recognition and Reward. Across each segment, meaningful impact is demonstrated through collaboration, partnership and sustained engagement with academics, students and institutional stakeholders. Together, the segments provide a structured approach to evidencing the breadth, depth and relational impact of LD practice. This interactive poster invites the ASCILITE community to inform what constitutes meaningful evidence of LD impact, drawing on diverse institutional contexts and practices across the sector. The poster itself is designed to be conversational, inviting delegates to contribute their perspectives by responding to three reflective prompts: What evidence do you think demonstrates the value of relationships and human connection in LD? What contributions of LDs have you noticed are often overlooked or invisible? What evidence do you see as most important in the future? Using pens and markers, or sticky notes, delegates will collectively build a visual representation of the evidence they value, the invisible work they recognise and the future directions they envision for the profession. This participatory approach reflects the framework’s emphasis on co-creation, reflective practice and shared understanding while creating opportunities for meaningful discussion among delegates from diverse institutional contexts. By the conclusion of the conference, the poster will have evolved into a collective representation of how the LD community values evidence, relationships, and impact. In doing so, it will demonstrate that the future of LD is not defined solely by digital technologies, but by the human connections that enable educational transformation.

Some environmental regulators now trigger restrictions on forecasts before exceedances occur, while machine-learning methods are proposed for the forecasting pipelines behind them. Delhi-NCR’s Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) directs advance invocation on numerical air-quality forecasts, yet reported practice often followed observed readings. Judicial and regulatory directions demand anticipatory action, yet none reviewed here specifies the confidence a forecast must carry before it justifies coercion. This article asks what validation, reproducibility and uncertainty-quantification thresholds an AI-enabled forecast must meet before triggering binding restrictions. Using a functional comparative method, it separates physics-based forecasts and digital dissemination from the machine-learning layer that makes a pipeline AI-enabled. GRAP, with the Supreme Court’s timing orders, is the single test case. Instruments from India, China, France and California’s air districts are coded for observed, forecast-based and discretionary triggers and read alongside forecast-verification studies. This article argues that proportionality and reasoned decision-making require restrictions to reflect forecast confidence as well as predicted severity, and that precaution licenses early action only if uncertainty is disclosed. One implication is that legal reliance on an AI-enabled forecast should depend on a disclosed validation dossier, because machine-learning layers add opacity and drift. Disclosure supports human oversight and lets affected people contest restrictions built on overconfident models. The contribution is a test mapping calibrated confidence onto the intensity of proportionality review. The assessment is prospective and doctrinal, evaluating design adequacy rather than operational performance; conclusions remain contingent.

The nature of posttraumatic growth (PTG), defined as positive changes that can occur after a traumatic event (TE), is debated due to its complex and dynamic relationship with psychological adjustment. Although heterogeneous PTG trajectories have been identified, the processes underlying their development over time remain insufficiently understood. This study, adopting a person-centred approach, seeks to identify latent classes with distinct multivariate trajectories (PTG, PTSD, positive thinking, deliberate rumination) over 1 year and their sociodemographic, event-related, and psychosocial determinants. A sample of 244 adults exposed to a TE completed, at three points spaced 6 months apart, online questionnaires assessing PTG and psychosocial variables. Sociodemographic and event-related characteristics were collected at baseline. Latent classes with distinct multivariate trajectories were identified. Analyses of variance, chi-square tests, and multinomial logistic regression tested differences between classes and their predictors. Three classes emerged: Constructive PTG (25%), Struggling PTG (45.5%), and No PTG (29.5%). Differences between classes were observed in age, coping, challenge to core beliefs, positive illusions, depression, and social support. Lower baseline adaptive coping predicted membership in the Struggling and No PTG groups, whereas lower challenge to core beliefs predicted the No PTG class. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of trajectories following lifetime trauma and the role of coping and cognitive engagement processes in the evolution of PTG over time. By integrating multiple processes within a longitudinal, person-centred framework, this study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of the perceived PTG.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is expected to revolutionise Australian’s economy with the potential to generate up to $600 billion per annum to GDP by 2030 (Australian Government, Department of Industry, Science and Resources, 2024). To keep up with the accelerating growth of AI, the higher education sector needs to transition from traditional teaching models to an AI-integrated pedagogy. One of the key concerns in this transition is to ensure equitable and sustainable adoption of AI in higher education. This concern is in line with the UNESCO’s recommendation on the ethics of AI (UNESCO,2021). AI adoption in higher education is both complex and consequential, as it may affect educational ethics through economic disparities among students and heterogenous student attitudes towards task fulfillment (Oxfam, 2022; Vacarelu, 2023). Moreover, it is reframing teaching, learning and assessment design, making it increasing difficult to distinguish between authentic effort, mastery, and output (Mills et al., 2025). Undertaken at an Australian university, this research project aims to addresses two pressing questions in contemporary higher education: how students are currently using generative AI (GenAI) for everyday learning tasks, their attitudes towards it and their AI readiness to support transition towards equitable and sustainable engagement with these tools. By revealing these issues, this project ensures student voices are central to ongoing debates about AI in higher education. Hence, this study is both equity-focused and evidenced-based as it responds to a critical gap for evidence-based insights to inform institutional policy development for a more equitable and sustainable digital ecosystem. Best practice suggests that when policies affecting students are designed with their involvement as co-designers, outcomes significantly improve. Therefore, framed as Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) research, the project places reflective practice and systematic inquiry at the heart of continuous improvement in teaching and learning outcomes. This study uses a quantitative survey method, whereby a structured questionnaire was administered during semester one, 2026. The questionnaire design is based on the Digital Divide and Self-regulated Learning framework. Data were collected from Humanities students across Law, Accounting, Business, and Education disciplines. Results reveal widespread adoption (98%), with some of it uncritical and potentially over-reliant (similar to Palmer, 2023). Notably, outliers exist where students refuse to use the tools entirely. Overall, findings indicate variation in GenAI usage, attitudes, access, and competence, suggesting the need for targeted interventions to advance equitable and sustainable AI integration. The findings are useful as they inform student-centred teaching practices, curriculum design, and policy frameworks aligned with the university’s commitment to innovative, ethical, and inclusive education.

Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

Agile project teams promote autonomy, yet little is known about how individuals actually experience autonomy in their day-to-day work. Building on a multiple-case study of five organisations in a manufacturing context with 61 semi-structured interviews, this study analyzes how individuals experience autonomy in agile project work. Drawing on the critical incident technique, complemented by an associative imagery technique, the paper presents a conceptual model of the action area of experienced autonomy, which unfolds through seven interrelated themes: decision-making, owning, realising, information sharing, learning, supporting, and team organising. The analysis of five cases shows how individuals make sense of this action area, revealing autonomy as a relational, contextual, and situational phenomenon. This study contributes to research on autonomy in management research by advancing the understanding of relational autonomy in agile project teams. It highlights autonomy as an experienced action area rather than a static job design feature or motivational characteristic. For managers structuring agile work in production and engineering environments, the findings offer a diagnostic lens to reflect on and support autonomy, fostering a motivating work context. Methodological contribution is achieved by demonstrating the value of associative imagery in capturing abstract and partly tacit aspects of work experience in agile production and engineering contexts.

This preregistration describes Experiment 2 of the Value-Recontextualizing Decision Support (VRDS) project, a PhD study at Florida Institute of Technology. Decision-support systems are usually judged by the quality of the outcome they recommend, rarely by whether a decision fits the decision-maker's own values. VRDS treats a choice that goes against a person's earlier values as a signal worth examining. It uses two mechanisms. Cognitive Value Recontextualization (CVR) shows such a choice from another point of view: a different framing of the situation, and a person affected by the choice. Adaptive Preference Alignment (APA) asks the person to clarify their priorities before the system updates its picture of their values. In the project's first experiment (N = 52), the full CVR+APA condition gave the highest value consistency without a measurable loss in performance. This experiment tests whether that holds in a larger sample and across several moral domains. Design. An online, between-subjects experiment with four conditions in a 2 × 2 design (CVR present or absent × APA present or absent): CVR+APA, CVR only, APA only, and Baseline (neither mechanism). The server assigns each participant to the condition with the fewest participants so far, so the four conditions stay balanced. All participants first answer four short blocks that measure their values. They then make choices in six moral scenarios: a chemical-leak evacuation, a wildfire evacuation, a limited cancer-treatment allocation, cuts to home-care visits inside an employer's rules, the same cuts decided by someone else, and a city repair rule chosen behind a veil of ignorance. Finally they see a summary of their own choices and answer feedback questions. The study takes at least 35 minutes. Participants. 104 adults recruited and paid through Prolific (26 per condition), plus students of one artificial intelligence course at Florida Tech who may take part for course credit (about 50). Hypotheses and expected outcomes. 23 hypotheses in four families, each with one primary hypothesis. (A) Conditions: participants in CVR+APA will make choices more consistent with their own values (Value Consistency Index, VCI) than participants in Baseline. (B) Position: how far a choice departs from a person's values will differ between deciding the care-visit cuts inside an employer's rules and receiving the same cuts decided by someone else. (C) Prediction: the system's Moral Prediction Function will predict the rule each participant chooses behind the veil of ignorance, before seeing the prediction, more often than chance (25%). (D) Performance: when a first pick goes against the participant's values and a reflection, clarification or confirmation step follows, the final choice will perform equivalently to the first choice (within ±5 points on a 0-100 scale). The four primary hypotheses are Holm-corrected together.
