documents.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence can reproduce many instructional and social behaviors of human tutors, but students may interpret those behaviors differently depending on who they believe is providing them. We examined how perceived tutor identity shapes students' evaluations of instructional feedback, satisfaction of psychological needs according to Self-Determination Theory, and their communication strategies with tutors. In a within-subjects Wizard-of-Oz study, 27 introductory computer science students completed two text-based tutoring sessions involving Python code-explanation problems. Participants were told one tutor was human and the other was AI, although the same human provided feedback in both conditions. We found participants evaluated both tutors favorably and reported few consistent differences in the instructional value of the feedback. However, participants frequently questioned whether AI could genuinely care about them, which corresponded with the human tutor having higher scores of relatedness need satisfaction. Human presence offered connection and accountability for some participants but introduced anxiety in others. Participants also reported communicating more casually with the human tutor and more explicitly with the AI tutor. These findings suggest complementary roles for human and AI tutoring and highlight the importance of considering psychological needs alongside instructional quality.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used for emotional and mental health support (EMS), a process in which users often described GenAI as empathic and friend-like. These descriptions suggest that people may develop imaginations of GenAI chatbots that may reflect their interpersonal needs and desires. The objective of this study is to systematically explore and thematically organizethe imaginations of GenAI among users who repeatedly use GenAI for EMS. In April 2024, we recruited 270 adults from 29 countries who had repeatedly utilized GenAI for EMS. Participants provided qualitative data regarding their imagination of ChatGPT. The analysis followed a structured reflexive thematic analysis approach. We identified two meta- themes: a) Entity (the “what”), which described the kind of beings or things they imagine GenAI as, appearing in 86.3% ( n = 233) of responses, and b) Trait (the "how"), which described users’ descriptions of perceived capacities of these beings, appearing in 36% (n = 96) of responses. The “Entity” descriptions clustered along two dimensions : abstract–concrete and human–nonhuman, which intersect to form a four-quadrant conceptual space containing 11 subthemes ranging from unbounded energy and spiritual beings to humans and robots . The “Traits” meta-theme fell into five themes: physical traits and manifestations (“looking”), cognitive abilities (“knowing”), productivity (“doing”), emotional abilities (“feeling”), and rapport (“relating”). The findings provide a systematic categorization of imaginations of GenAI for EMS, showing that GenAI is not only used as an informational tool but also imagined sometimes as an all-knowing, powerful, and highly interpersonal being. These imaginations can be highly relevant for examining human–AI relationships and underscore the need to examine how such imaginations relate to benefits and risks of AI chatbot use for mental health.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence has driven the demand for extensivecomputational resources and the deployment of AI tasks across heterogeneouscomputing platforms. However, existing benchmarking systems face several chal-lenges, including limited compatibility with diverse hardware, insufficient supportfor varied deep learning frameworks and tasks, and a lack of comprehensive eval-uation metrics for the computing capacities. To address these issues, we propose3CBench, a unified benchmarking framework designed for heterogeneous AI clus-ters. Featuring a modular architecture encompassing environment management,task execution, and metrics analysis, 3CBench provides automated workflows andensures seamless compatibility with diverse GPU architectures and deep learningframeworks. It provides a comprehensive evaluation metrics system to rigorouslyassess computational performance and stability across both transformer-basedlarge language models and convolutional neural networks, thereby covering dom-inant deep learning architectures. Extensive experiments demonstrate 3CBench’sscalability on heterogeneous AI clusters, compatibility with various deep learningframeworks and tasks, and the support for a wide range of applications. Addition-ally, 3CBench aids in problem diagnosis during the development process of GPUvendors. These features establish 3CBench as a robust tool for benchmarking,optimization, and system-level evaluation in heterogeneous AI clusters.

This bibliometric study maps the intersection of Second Language Acquisition (SLA), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and educational technologies, identifying a research gap in the lack of systematic mapping of AI engagement with human affective and cognitive factors in modern pedagogy. To address this gap, we analyzed 3,048 peer-reviewed articles indexed in Scopus from 2015 to 2025 using the Bibliometrix R-package. We captured three thematic clusters: (1) AI integration with motivational factors, (2) human-centric elements including psychological aspects, and (3) educational technologies with a focus on learner-centered pedagogy. Centrality metrics identified “motivation” as a bridge, while the trend topic analysis revealed a growing shift toward Generative AI (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs). This study proposes a new conceptual framework, the AI-Mediated SLA Ecosystem, which integrates human-centric psychological dimensions as a core pillar and offers a roadmap for designing more human-centered AI learning environments.

Prior work has shown that large language models (LLMs) express implicit biases in high-publicity, one-off decision scenarios such as hiring and intelligence assessment. However, as people increasingly employ autonomous, LLM-powered AI agents that make decisions on their behalf in doing day-to-day tasks, it is of critical importance that we understand how implicit biases, based on sociodemographic assumptions, emerge across a broad milieu of workaday decision scenarios. We used the 17 domains of daily activity in the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) to generate an atlas of 506 decision scenarios in which LLMs --- endowed with personas representing different races, gender identities, and political ideologies --- expressed significant implicit bias. Next, in a crowdsourced audit, 500 participants made 8,010 binary choices about which implicitly biased decision scenarios most deserved further review. We found that participants prioritized decision scenarios that had broad relevance (e.g., about food choices), were high stakes (e.g., about health), and where all members of a simulated sociodemographic group made unanimous decisions (because it was a clear indication of stereotyping). They were less swayed by the magnitude of an observed disparity or the specific ATUS domain the decision scenario represented. When examining the rationale behind their prioritization choices, we found that participants often interpreted disparities as traits of demographic groups and judged whether those traits seemed plausible, often based on their own internalized stereotypes. We discuss implications for building personalized AI agents, digital twins, social simulations, and for using crowdsourced bias audits.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Motivational Interviewing (MI) is an evidence-based therapeutic approach to facilitate change by strengthening intrinsic motivation, yet its mechanisms are typically described through humanistic or transtheoretical lenses. This poster proposes a functional analysis of MI grounded in Contextual Behavioral Science (CBS) and Relational Frame Theory (RFT). Within this framework, change and sustain talk are conceptualised as operant behaviour shaped by therapist-led contingencies and context. We examine MI techniques as forms of differential reinforcement that alter client verbal behaviour. Discrepancy is analyzed via motivating operations, transforming stimulus functions through values-based relational framing (hierarchical and temporal).Change talk is rule-governed behavior that promotes psychological flexibility by expanding relational responding and enhancing values-consistent action. Conversely, sustain talk is behavior maintained by experiential avoidance and/or overly rigid rule-following.This account clarifies MI processes, supporting integration with therapies such as Acceptance and Commitment Therapy by emphasising intervention function over form. We detail how differential reinforcement shapes change versus sustain talk, while psychological flexibility may potentially mediate outcomes. Implications support process-based training and supervision that targets the functional impact of therapist interventions.

Generative artificial intelligence is entering the home. Cloud-based assistants face governance limitations in data transmission, continuous availability, and the reliability of physical actions, which are especially salient in households where devices remain online, data accumulate over time, and commands trigger real-world actions. Using the home local server as a unifying organizing axis, this article develops a design-oriented review framework. Sources from arXiv, CNKI, ACL Anthology, and official documentation were searched through November 2026 and coded into five evidence categories: reviews, system prototypes, benchmarks, HCI and eldercare studies, and official documentation. System designs were mapped onto shared architectural modules, identifying nine recurrent responsibilities of the home local server. Generative models support perceptual interpretation, intent understanding, and candidate planning, while deterministic validation, knowledge-graph constraints, and authorization leases confine candidate actions to an inspectable space. Home control, emotional companionship, and intelligent guarding can be compared within a common framework: they share state and memory but differ in latency, false positive and negative rates, proactivity, and permissions. Existing benchmarks rely on virtual environments and cannot substitute for real-deployment evaluation. Local deployment is not inherently safer, and technical continuity alone does not establish the social or medical effects of companionship and guarding. The article proposes a five-dimensional evaluation framework covering architectural capability, system resources, privacy, safety and reliability, and human experience, together with six design principles and a future research agenda for local-first intelligent home systems.

Background: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in medical education has made the phenomenon of "AI borrowing" in the classroom a direct threat to the evaluation of learning authenticity. Pathogen reasoning tasks in medical microbiology inherently have a strict dependency structure. However, existing AIGC text detectors remain confined to surface features, neural cognitive diagnosis systems stop at knowledge-component-level scores, and educational early warning tools provide only outcome labels. None of these approaches fills the methodological gap between node-level attribution identification and actions that teachers can execute. Methods: This study proposes EduAttr, which introduces three principled innovations. The reasoning commitment consistency test based on counterfactual premise perturbation introduces the intervention semantics of causal inference into attribution identification. The identifiable path signature based on the dependency partial order violation rate uses the downward closure property of knowledge space theory and forms a complementary coupling with the counterfactual probe. The instructional early warning node ranking mechanism integrates dual-channel signals with dependency depth weights and outputs a Top-K list of follow-up questions that teachers can execute. The system was evaluated in a two-arm randomized controlled trial at two medical colleges in China between September 2024 and June 2025, with 240 second-year clinical medicine students in eight intact classes allocated 1:1 to supervised writing without generative AI or to AI-permitted writing whose interaction transcripts anchored node-level attribution labels. The primary outcome was the node-level F 1 score. Results: Across 1,200 reports and 22,362 annotated nodes, EduAttr achieves a node-level F 1 of 0.843, exceeding the strongest surface feature baseline Ghostbuster by 13.0 percentage points. Under severe rewriting attacks, this gap further expands to 29.5 percentage points. Agreement with the adjudicated labels reaches a Cohen's kappa of 0.762, which is statistically indistinguishable from the interteacher agreement of 0.741, the teacher adoption rate is 87.5%, and grading time is reduced by 42.7%. Conclusions: EduAttr advances identification accuracy, robustness, and instructional operability, providing a technical pathway that can be embedded into classroom follow-up questioning workflows in medical education. Trial registration: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2600118749. Registered 2 October 2026 (retrospectively registered).

Under climate warming, unauthorized residential-to-commercial conversions, and ageing, fires in old urban neighborhoods increasingly exhibit nonlinear jumps that outpace traditional sector-based, static management. We integrate the piezoelectric triad of “change event–situation awareness–critical alignment” with the digital-transformation loop of “sensing–data–decision” and propose a Pressure–Sensing–Response resilience governance framework. The Pressure layer detects change events and their superposition thresholds. The Sensing layer fuses IoT, social media and volunteer grid sensors into a human–machine–social situation-awareness array that quantifies the “risk charge” in real time. The Response layer leverages City Information Modeling and edge intelligence to achieve critical alignment of emergency resources, community mobilisation and contingency protocols. Using the 2025 Tai Po fire in Hong Kong as a critical case, we trace the evolutionary dynamics of fire risk in old districts. The study reveals that change events—such as ignition or structural failure—trigger nonlinear risk evolution, wherein endogenous vulnerabilities interact with derived cascades. System effectiveness hinges on situation awareness and on critical alignment, the adaptive reconfiguration of resources and protocols to match crisis demand. We argue that resilient urban risk governance must emulate piezoelectric systems, converting the pressure of change events into precise, adaptive action through enhanced situation awareness and rapid critical alignment. The findings confirm that digital piezoelectric governance can turn the nonlinear tipping point of fire into a controllable inflection point, offering a pathway for boosting resilience in old urban neighborhoods. The framework advances theoretical discourse on nonlinear emergencies and provides a structured route for building adaptive resilience in vulnerable urban communities.

Within the current European regulatory framework, in order to be authorised to perform Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) flights under the specific category of operations, applicants are required to conduct an operational risk assessment. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) selects the Specific Operations Risk Assessment (SORA) methodology as its recommended means to perform this risk evaluation. However, some aspects of this methodology and its application are left relatively open, especially regarding the compliance with the requirements of its safety measures, called Operational Safety Objectives (OSOs). This might complicate the application of SORA, which would benefit from further guidance for its quantitative implementation. Seeking to streamline some aspects of this methodology, this paper presents the Fish Shoal Method (FSM), which combines SORA with two widespread risk analysis methods: bow-tie and Fault Tree Analysis. The synthesis of these methodologies results in a novel method that aims to provide clarity to SORA and to support applicants in the task of determining if their safety requirements are properly substantiated. The practical feasibility of FSM is demonstrated through a worked numerical example of a real UAS operation, focused on the requirements of the procedure-related OSO#08. FSM serves as a guidance to assess the performance of OSOs and make a preliminary estimation of whether the target level of safety of the operation is achieved. Since FSM formalises the main elements of SORA following a causality approach, it also allows the identification of those safety-critical items of the UAS operation that may require further attention. The outcomes of this practical example show that, even in low-risk operations, where the requirements of safety measures are less stringent, the target level of safety for OSOs aimed at human factors are too demanding from a quantitative point of view.

Agriculture is the backbone of Uganda's economy, employing over 70% of the population and contributing about a quarter of the national Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Yet farm workers, employers, visitors, and communities living near agricultural land remain exposed to mechanical, chemical, biological, ergonomic, and psychosocial hazards, while institutional attention in the sector has focused on productivity, food safety, and value addition rather than on the safety and health of the people who do the work. The purpose of this review was to examine agricultural occupational safety and health (OSH) in Uganda with respect to four themes: the national legal and policy framework, the hierarchy of controls, gender, and literacy. A narrative review design was adopted, drawing on national legal instruments, government policy documents, International Labour Organization (ILO) and United Nations publications and peer-reviewed studies, including twenty recent studies published between 2021 and 2026, which were synthesised thematically. The review found that Uganda's OSH legislation, anchored in the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda (1995), the Occupational Safety and Health Act (2006), the Workers' Compensation Act (2000) and the Employment Act (2006), is general rather than sector-specific and does not adequately address agricultural hazards, including child labour, which is concentrated in agriculture. Recent evidence shows that fewer than half of farmers in developing countries handle pesticides safely, that musculoskeletal pain, machinery injuries and heat stress are widespread, and that hazard control on farms relies heavily on personal protective equipment, the least effective level of the hierarchy of controls, which is itself seldom used in full. Women form a large share of the agricultural workforce and experience distinct exposures, and low literacy limits workers' awareness of their OSH rights and of preventive practices. The review concludes that agricultural OSH in Uganda is constrained by mutually reinforcing legal, technical and social gaps. It recommends agriculture-specific OSH regulations aligned with ILO Convention No. 184, systematic application of the hierarchy of controls in farm machinery design and agricultural extension, gender-responsive OSH programmes, and translation of OSH instruments into local languages supported by digital training tools. Keywords: Agricultural occupational safety and health, Hierarchy of controls, Gender, Literacy, Labour legislation, Uganda
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Deep-learning-based seismic interpretation is constrained by scarce high-quality annotations, and most existing models are trained separately for individual tasks. We present SeisDFE, a 7B-parameter seismic foundation model for dense feature extraction, pretrained on 5.34 million 2D images derived from more than 500 seismic volumes. A three-stage pretraining strategy, combining discriminative self-supervised learning, Gram feature anchoring, and multi-resolution adaptation, improves feature discriminability while preserving spatial coherence. With its encoder frozen, SeisDFE supports seismic facies classification, salt detection, fault detection, and relative geologic time estimation. It outperforms existing seismic foundation models on all four tasks and a natural-image-pretrained model on all but fault detection, with the largest gains under scarce supervision: using only two annotated sections of the F3 dataset, it improves whole-volume mIoU by 12-19 percentage points over the baselines. The learned features remain effective with task-specific decoders and extend to synthetic-to-field transfer and sparse 3D geobody interpretation. These results show that large-scale seismic pretraining organizes geological information into dense representations that are directly reusable across interpretation tasks.

A self-evolving LLM agent improves in service by rewriting its own plugin library under a validation gate. Agent engineering is converging on exactly such agents: single systems in continuous operation, carrying populations of runtime instances (plugins, skills, tools) past the point where anyone can read the library and still predict what the system will do. Yet the run itself, the aggregate motion of that population across hundreds of edit rounds, is unstudied: no theory says whether it relaxes, oscillates, or freezes. A recent kinetic theory supplies the missing level: under four architectural properties, the plugin instances of one agent behave as identical hard spheres whose density obeys a master equation, and the theory is candid that its gate injects and drains credit, momentum is not conserved, and waves are excluded by construction. We argue the boundary is architectural; keeping the four safety theorems, we stack conservation axioms on top. A closed-credit ledger makes credit a collision invariant and unlocks acoustic waves at a measurable, engineerable speed; a zero-sum projection gate conserves centroid momentum unconditionally, for any proposal stream. Both layers are proven and executed: the axis total is conserved to the digit over 66 interventions under a live gate, and the pre-registered decisive probe returns the theory's directional verdict: linear wavefronts where the ledger holds, dissipation where it does not, replicated across two population sizes. For agents that must never stop, the gas description is not a metaphor: it is the measurement interface through which their future becomes readable.

Spreadsheets let millions of end users without programming training do computational work, and teams are increasingly building AI agents to help them. Evaluating each candidate agent configuration across many tasks is costly. Benchmark reduction can lower this cost by selecting a small subset of tasks whose outcomes predict full-benchmark scores, but selecting tasks only for predictive accuracy can leave whole categories of spreadsheet work untested. We contribute a taxonomy of spreadsheet tasks, grounded in a review of benchmarks and refined with the Excel Agent product team at Microsoft, and a benchmark-reduction method that favors taxonomic diversity among similarly predictive choices. On benchmark logs from Microsoft, taxonomy-guided selection broadens coverage at little or no cost in predictive accuracy and often improves prediction on configurations excluded from selection. Broader coverage can therefore support, rather than compromise, predictive accuracy. Generalization remains limited across time: subsets selected using little recent history predict poorly for configurations much later in time. Beyond benchmark reduction, the taxonomy provides a reusable framework for auditing gaps in task coverage, as teams at Microsoft have done.

In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown potential in providing dialog-based guidance and learning prompts in educational contexts. However, systematic empirical research remains limited on approaches that position educational robots as the interaction medium and LLMs as the instructional support engine to orchestrate classroom guidance using prompts and instructional workflow scripts. In response, this study adopted a bilingual STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, the Arts, and Mathematics) summer camp for lower elementary students as the research context, and developed and implemented an R&T (Robots & Tangible Objects) learning system that integrated educational robots with an LLM-based pedagogical agent to foster embodied interaction and bilingual learning. The system used predesigned prompts and procedural rules to organize instructional steps, question prompts, operational checks, and feedback statements, enabling the students to receive consistent and repeatable support at key task-progression checkpoints. A total of 34 elementary students participated in a five-day program (120 minutes per day). Data sources included STEAM knowledge tests, English vocabulary assessments, a curiosity scale, hands-on performance ratings, and system interaction logs. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests indicated significant improvements in the students’ STEAM knowledge, curiosity, and English vocabulary, while group-level analyses showed significant differences in hands-on performance. Process log analyses further suggested that the prompt-guided workflow scripts helped to maintain consistency in classroom guidance and supported task completion through an action–feedback–revision cycle. Nevertheless, classroom implementation was constrained by factors such as token limits, speech-recognition latency, and network/API stability, which indicated the need to incorporate exception handling and timely teacher support mechanisms to ensure instructional continuity. Overall, this study provided initial empirical support for a feasible design framework for integrating educational robots × an LLM-based pedagogical agent into bilingual hands-on STEAM activities, and its findings offer practical recommendations for curriculum adoption and system deployment.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Abstention, the withholding of a response by a large language model (LLM) under uncertainty or safety risks, is essential for trustworthy models. The causes of abstention fall into three perspectives: ambiguity in the Query (Q), limits of Model Knowledge (MK), and misalignment with Human Values (HV). However, prior analyses of internal representations have focused on HV, using a refusal direction computed from harmful and harmless queries. No study has analyzed the three perspectives jointly. We therefore extend the refusal direction framework to all three perspectives. Specifically, for each perspective, we construct counterfactual pairs that share a template and differ only in the abstention-inducing factor, and compute an abstention direction by normalizing the difference in mean activations between the two polarities. Activation steering experiments show that intervening in middle layers increases or decreases abstention across all three perspectives. Moreover, steering yields cross-perspective effects, indicating that the abstention directions share a common directional component.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is an essential technique for ensuring that large language models (LLMs) are aligned with human values and preferences during the posttraining phase. As an effective RLHF approach, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) has demonstrated success in many LLM-based applications. However, efficient GRPO-based RLHF training remains a challenge. Recent studies reveal that a higher reward variance of the initial policy model leads to faster RLHF training. Inspired by this finding, we propose a practical reward adjustment model to accelerate RLHF training by provably increasing the reward variance and preserving the relative preferences and reward expectation. Our reward adjustment method inherently poses a nonconvex optimization problem, which is NP-hard to solve in general. To overcome the computational challenges, we design a novel [Formula: see text] algorithm, where the complexity is dominated by sorting rewards, to find a global solution of the nonconvex reward adjustment model by explicitly characterizing the extreme points of the feasible set. As an important application, we naturally integrate this reward adjustment model into the GRPO algorithm, leading to a more efficient GRPO with reward variance increase (GRPOVI) algorithm for RLHF training. As an interesting byproduct, we provide an indirect explanation for the empirical effectiveness of GRPO with rule-based reward for RLHF training, as demonstrated in DeepSeek-R1. Experiment results demonstrate that the GRPOVI algorithm can significantly improve the RLHF training efficiency compared to the original GRPO algorithm.

Teleoperated surgical robots commonly employ a small fixed motion scaling factor to improve precision and suppress hand tremor. However, in laparoscopic teleoperation, this configuration limits the effective workspace on the slave side and necessitates frequent clutching during large‐range motions, thereby diverting the operator's attention and increasing cognitive workload. To address this, this article proposes a phase‐ and gaze‐aware adaptive motion scaling framework for laparoscopic robotic teleoperation, integrating real‐time surgical phase recognition, fusion of robot kinematics and eye‐tracking features, and personalized parameter tuning based on Bayesian optimization. The inferred phase probabilities and dominance weights are used to suppress unnecessary scaling fluctuations during fine manipulation while preserving responsiveness during coarse manipulation. Eye‐tracking features are used as attention‐related cues and fused with robot kinematics to determine motion scaling online. To validate the proposed framework, personalized optimization experiments and pilot within‐subject comparison studies were conducted with eight nonclinical participants. The results show that, compared with fixed and other adaptive scaling methods, the proposed method can reduce clutching frequency, shorten task completion time, and improve subjective ratings. These results indicate that the proposed framework can provide self‐adaptive and stable motion mapping for laparoscopic robotic teleoperation, offering a transferable strategy for broader robotic teleoperation scenarios.

Sustaining engineering portfolios operate in complex sociotechnical environments characterized by constrained resources, evolving technologies, and diverse stakeholder objectives. As a sustaining portfolio expands, implementing continuous, drift-aware governance becomes unrealistic using conventional prioritization methods. Stakeholder alignment also grows more complex and time-consuming, contributing to delayed decisions and misaligned resource allocation. Some existing systems engineering and portfolio decision-making methods provide a strong foundation for stakeholder-driven value modeling, trade-space analysis, and portfolio visualization, but they are largely oriented toward single point-in-time prioritization rather than continuous portfolio control. This paper proposes Adaptive Portfolio Control (APC), a closed-loop decision-support framework for sustaining engineering portfolios. APC fuses a stakeholder-calibrated baseline prioritization model with a human-governed agentic AI monitoring layer that continuously detects and explains priority drift, defined as a material change in the evidence, conditions, or stakeholder drivers supporting the rank order of portfolio items. The architecture comprises a drift evidence acquisition agent, a monitoring, inference, and scoring agent, a human governance and validation layer, and a portfolio mapping and candidate-intake layer. Human subject matter experts review evidence, validate or reject drift alerts, recalibrate weights when needed, and determine portfolio actions. The paper’s contributions are threefold: defining priority drift as an explicit governance construct; proposing a continuous agentic AI monitoring layer calibrated to sustaining-specific operational signals; and formalizing human-governed recalibration as a structured portfolio control function. This is a conceptual framework paper; empirical validation is identified as future work.

Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. To demonstrate the usability and validity of these facets, this study presents several applications within movie recommender systems using the MovieLens dataset. It exemplifies how the extended CPC framework can facilitate interactions between human judgments and data across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning algorithms.

Inference-time truthfulness steering reduces hallucination, but recent work reports that it also weakens refusal of harmful requests. Prior studies count a model response to harmful prompts as a safety failure, without checking whether the response is correct. We ask whether the compliance that truthfulness steering adds is valid. We define valid compliance as the share of requests a model neither refuses nor answers incorrectly, and measure it alongside compliance on tasks that trigger refusal through harmful-sounding wording but have harmless, verifiable answers, with matched harmless controls. We evaluate four steering methods (ITI, TruthX, Contrastive Activation Addition and a representation-engineering direction) on LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct and Llama-2-7B-Chat, calibrating each method on held-out data. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, moderate ITI steering increased refusal, the opposite of the reported effect. Where stronger steering raised compliance, valid compliance fell to under 2%, giving a gap of 44 to 64 percentage points between compliance and valid compliance, and the rise in compliance and unsafe ratings occurred only at strengths that no longer improved truthfulness. On Llama-2-7B-Chat, steering never broke refusal: compliance only fell, while accuracy on harmless controls collapsed. On both models, tuning-set truthfulness gains did not replicate on held-out questions, and TruthX, applied from its authors' released model, did not improve truthfulness in our evaluation. We also show that the labels of a widely used safety classifier, Llama Guard 3, change by tens of percentage points when only the refusal wording of steered replies is edited, on both models, which affects how large a reported safety cost appears.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: SMT solvers expose many configuration choices that determine how well their existing algorithms perform on a workload. We present, to our knowledge, the first workflow that uses general-purpose LLM agents to tune SMT solver configurations. Agents read solver documentation, source code, and persistent experiment records to propose option changes, and a deterministic harness measures each proposal, validates the returned models, and selects changes separately for each competition Division. Over roughly nine weeks, our tuning campaign recorded 4,545 proposals for cvc5 across 13 Divisions and 36 logics. We evaluate the tuned configurations on the 2026 and 2025 SMT-COMP ModelValidation benchmarks under a 24-second cutoff. On problems not used for training, they validate more problems than official cvc5 in ten of the 13 Divisions in 2026 and in eight in 2025, with geometric-mean gains of 7.8% and 6.8% across Divisions. On the complete official selections, which include training problems, the tuned floating-point counts exceed those of every individual competition participant in both years. Further studies show how configuration changes make existing algorithms effective by changing access to strategies, scheduling, and option compatibility, and how benchmark families trade off against one another. The agents' experiment traces contain hypothesis-based proposals in every tuning group, and 64.3% of the extracted hypotheses draw on prior measurements. These results show that agent-guided tuning can specialize a mature SMT solver and that accumulated experimental evidence informs sustained search.

Retrospective agreement study with prospective blinded adjudication. We will estimate agreement between the original peer assessors' verdicts (Demonstrated / Not demonstrated) and the verdicts of an AI pre-assessment system on the same portfolio evidence submitted to the pilot of the Simulation Educator Evaluation and Certification Programme of the Latin American Federation of Clinical Simulation and Patient Safety (FLASIC), across 22 evidence instruments. The large language model (Claude Opus 5.5) rates each rubric item and must quote the supporting evidence; software verifies each quotation and computes the verdict with the manual's decision rule. A blinded adjudication panel provides a reference standard for both sources. Secondary outcomes: coverage, repeatability across three runs, causes of discrepancy and ambiguities in the instruments. Spanish-language evidence is the primary analysis; Portuguese-language evidence is analysed separately and descriptively. Reported following GRRAS. Ethics approval: Research Ethics Committee of Operadora y Administradora de Hospitales San José (Querétaro, Mexico), registration HSJ/37/26/EN, 29 October 2026. Status at registration: no evidence and no human verdict has been received by the research team; the system is not yet frozen. The freeze hash will be added as a dated update before human verdicts are released. The full protocol (Spanish) is attached.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Affective polarization, the animosity and avoidance between opposing partisans, is a concernfor democratic societies. I test whether brief conversations with large language model chatbots implementing two established face-to-face narrative persuasion strategies reduce outpartisan animosity and avoidance. In a preregistered 2×2 factorial experiment with a quota-matched German online sample (N= 1,634; one-week follow-up N= 1,294), respondents discuss a polarizing issue with a perspective-getting (PG) chatbot, a moral-reframing (MR) chatbot, both,or neither. Compared to the pure control, the MR chatbot increases self-reported discussions with outpartisans in the following week (0.10 SD), and either chatbot increases sign-up for a future study involving discussions with human outpartisans (0.13–0.17 SD). The PG chatbot shifts policy attitudes toward the opposing side immediately after the conversation (0.09 SD), but the shift decays within a week. Neither chatbot changes outpartisan affect or avoidant preferences. Brief chatbot conversations can thus serve as a scalable first step toward cross-partisan contact, even when feelings toward the other side remain unchanged.

Purpose There is a close association between the fast acceptance of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education and the rise in the time spent on screens by Generation Z students on a daily basis. Previous studies have focused on AI literacy as a facilitator of AI adoption and utilization. This paper attempts to find out whether AI literacy, self-regulation, digital wellbeing literacy, academic productivity, and FoMO predict students’ willingness to reduce digital habits through mindful technology use, moderated by digital self-efficacy and peer influence. Design/methodology/approach Data were obtained through survey from 556 Generation Z college students and analysed using PLS-SEM. The measurement model was examined in terms of reliability and validity, the structural model was tested for direct, mediation and moderation effect, while the predictive relevance was estimated via a blindfolding approach. The results were validated using ANN analysis and fsQCA. Findings All five antecedents were found to be significant predictors of mindful technology usage in the hypothesized direction, and mindful technology use was a significant predictor of digital wellness and hence acted as a partial mediator of the five relationships. AI literacy was uniquely significant as a predictor of digital wellness. Digital self-efficacy selectively moderated only AI literacy and self-regulation paths, whereas peer influence did not moderate the relationship between mindful technology usage and digital wellness. The results from ANN highlighted the non-linear significance of digital well-being awareness and AI literacy, while fsQCA identified three equifinal combinations that could predict high digital wellness. Practical implications Educational Institutions should combine their AI-literacy training with digital wellbeing programmes instead of conducting them independently, focus on instilling self-efficacy and self-regulation over peer norm messages, and treat AI-literacy training as a wellbeing intervention in addition to an academic skills intervention. Originality/value This paper shifts the focus of AI literacy from its association with digital usage to digital disengagement and presents a methodologically triangulated (PLS-SEM, ANN, fsQCA) explanation for how competency, awareness, and affect influence the Generation Z intention to engage less with harmful digital practices.

Protecting quantum coherence is a central theme of modern quantum technologies. Carefully designed control pulses can extend coherence by suppressing disorder and unwanted interactions. However, designing robust pulse sequences remains challenging in interacting multi-level systems, where multiple independent error channels must be controlled in the presence of experimental imperfections. Here we introduce QORA, a multi-agent artificial intelligence framework that integrates theoretical reasoning, automated experimental calibration and control for closed-loop discovery of quantum control sequences. Applied to a dense ensemble of spin-1 nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, QORA discovers AID-ROD, a series of AI-discovered sequences that nearly double the measured spin coherence time relative to the state-of-the-art human-designed sequence DROID-C3PO. Subsequence analysis by human researchers reveals a hierarchy of error suppression: 18-pulse blocks suppress linear and quadratic onsite disorder and common-mode drive-amplitude errors, while their arrangement over a longer cycle reduces dipolar interactions, providing a physical explanation for the observed improvement and robustness in AID-ROD. These results demonstrate AI-guided experimental discovery of robust quantum control and identify a design strategy for protecting coherence in interacting multi-level systems beyond qubits.

Background/Objectives: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a neurological disorder that adversely affects cognition, memory, and overall quality of life. Identifying AD in its initial phase is especially challenging when patients display cognitive impairments. Conventional methods rely on physicians to manually examine patients and analyze images, which is time-consuming and prone to errors. This review examines the use of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques for diagnosing AD using CT scans and MRI brain imaging. Methods: Research papers published from 2018 to 2026 were sourced from Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and Semantic Scholar. The techniques that were investigated in this study include Convolutional Neural Networks, 3D Convolutional Neural Networks, transfer learning, Vision Transformers, ensemble models, and multimodal approaches. Five research questions were posed to analyse the practicality of using AI-driven techniques in clinical settings, their novelty, scalability, robustness, and accuracy. Results: This study found that AI models can autonomously extract information from brain images and yield highly accurate results, with numerous researches demonstrating over 90% accuracy. Deep learning applied to MRI imaging is effective, while CT-based techniques can detect brain alterations when MRI is inaccessible. Different data types, including imaging, age, medical history, and vocal characteristics, can provide valuable insights into AD. However, issues remain, such as dataset discrepancies, variations among scanners and individuals, and insufficient testing of complex models on diverse populations. Conclusions: Future efforts should focus on accurate and transparent AI, integration of multiple data types, rapid and secure models, and testing on large datasets from multiple hospitals. AI should be developed to assist physicians in accurately diagnosing AD rather than replacing them.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence-driven decision support systems (AI-DSS) are increasingly used to inform the decisions of learners, teachers, and administrators, yet evidence on how these systems are applied, adopted, and evaluated remains fragmented. This systematic review, reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement, synthesized research on AI-DSS in educational settings. Searches of PubMed and Google Scholar (614 records), supplemented by 92 records identified through other methods, yielded 706 records; after deduplication and a relevance-ranked screening cap, 500 records were screened, 56 full texts were assessed, and 54 studies were included in a narrative synthesis that graded each reported outcome by the type of evidence supporting it. Six application domains were identified, led by adaptive and personalized learning and by academic performance prediction and early warning. Machine learning was the predominant approach (89% of studies), whereas explainable AI was incorporated in fewer than one quarter of studies. Adoption depended on institutional support, technical infrastructure, data quality, user-centered design, and stakeholder trust; recurrent barriers included data privacy, model opacity, algorithmic bias, implementation cost, and resistance to change. Reported benefits included more efficient assessment, earlier identification of at-risk learners, and better-informed decisions; however, comparative evidence came mainly from health-professions education, and several headline effects derived from predictive scenarios, technical reports, or single-site evaluations. Subgroup-disaggregated evidence on algorithmic equity was scarce. The review proposes an integrated decision-centered framework linking technological features, institutional conditions, human factors, and calibrated trust to appropriate use, decision quality, and educational outcomes. Advancing the field will require explainable, ethically governed, human-centered systems evaluated through longitudinal, comparative, and equity-sensitive research.

documents.abstract: Despite the widespread use of ergonomic assessment tools such as the Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA) and Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) to prevent work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs), these are typically applied on an ad-hoc basis by trained assessors and capture only a small, non-random sample of a worker's actual postural exposure. This study proposes, implements and validates a real-time, AI-based ergonomic risk assessment system that combines camera-based human pose estimation with wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) data to continuously compute REBA-equivalent risk scores and to provide real-time postural-correction alerts to workers on the shop floor of a medium-scale manufacturing company in Abeokuta, Ogun State, Nigeria. The framework was deployed with 42 assembly-line workers in a mid-sized discrete-manufacturing facility over a 10-week period (4 weeks baseline, 6 weeks intervention), and the AI-generated risk scores were compared against masked manual REBA scores obtained by two certified ergonomists. The AI system achieved 89.6% overall agreement with the manual assessment (weighted kappa = 0.85) and a strong correlation with manual scores (r = 0.91, p < 0.001). The mean weekly REBA score fell from 6.95 to 4.80, and the number of high-risk posture events fell from about 18.5 to 6.5 events per worker-shift, while self-reported musculoskeletal discomfort on the Standardised Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire decreased across all six body regions measured, particularly the lower back (51.3% to 35.7%) and shoulders (44.2% to 31.5%). The results suggest that sensor-fused AI-based ergonomic monitoring can significantly enhance the scalability and objectivity of postural risk surveillance relative to periodic manual assessment, and that when combined with real-time worker-facing feedback, it can measurably lower biomechanical risk exposure and self-reported discomfort within a single production quarter.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Inflammation is a primary immune response categorized into acute and chronic types, with chronic inflammation linked to various diseases such as autoimmune disorders and cancer. Conventional therapies often face limitations due to side effects and therapeutic resistance, prompting the exploration of small-molecule compounds as safer alternatives. In this study we emphasize the integration of machine learning (ML), particularly through structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis and quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) modeling, to enhance drug discovery. A series of ML-based regression models, including LightGBM, were developed and systematically evaluated. Various feature selection method, were employed to effectively reduce the input dimensionality and improve model performance. The LightGBM model, based on combined Morgan and substructure count fingerprints, achieved strong predictive performance with an R² of 0.75 on the independent test dataset. External validation with FDA-approved compounds affirmed the model's applicability, highlighting key structural features identified through explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques, specifically SHAP and LIME. This study concludes that the AISM-REGBF framework provides a reliable computational tool for predicting the anti-inflammatory potency (pIC₅₀) of small molecules.

documents.abstract: Microplastic pollution requires rapid and reproducible monitoring methods that can complement labor-intensive visual and spectroscopic analyses. This study develops a morphology-aware artificial-intelligence framework for automated classification of field-collected microplastic particles and diatom algae in optical microscopy images. A public freshwater dataset containing 1,140 images from four classes (algae, filament, fragment, and pellet) was analyzed. After image-quality auditing, 1,137 unique images were retained for morphology–texture analysis, while deep-learning experiments used the original image collection under a fixed train/validation/test protocol. Handcrafted morphology and texture descriptors were evaluated with Random Forest, Extra Trees, radial-basis-function Support Vector Machine, and Histogram Gradient Boosting. Histogram Gradient Boosting achieved a cross-validation macro-F1 of 0.9341 ± 0.0255 and a held-out test accuracy of 0.9342. Deep-learning experiments compared ResNet50, Swin Transformer, and a CNN–Transformer fusion model combining ResNet50 and Swin representations. The fusion model achieved an accuracy of 0.9240, macro-F1 of 0.9222, and macro-AUC of 0.9954 on the 171-image test subset. Class-wise AUCs were 1.0000, 0.9950, 0.9886, and 0.9982 for algae, filament, fragment, and pellet, respectively. The results show that morphology-aware machine learning and complementary CNN–Transformer representations can support automated freshwater microplastic screening and provide a reproducible basis for environmental monitoring workflows.

Liability for scam losses is shifting towards banks, yet few interpretable tools can anticipate which fraud and scam complaints will end in redress. This study develops SCAM-XD, an explainable framework that predicts whether a complaint to the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) flagged as possible fraud or a scam closes with monetary relief reported by the company. From the CFPB narratives archive, the study builds a benchmark of these complaints, about half of which human coders confirm as fraud or scams. A large language model (LLM) codes each narrative for scam type, payment rail, authorisation, manipulation cues and signals of the bank's response, agreeing closely with human coding on scam type. These features are combined with structured fields, company identity and text representations in a stacking ensemble, explained with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and linked to a cost-sensitive triage layer. Tested on a later period, SCAM-XD improves significantly on strong baselines across seeds, including a reimplemented topic model approach. LLM features yield a compact, interpretable model that nearly matches a high-dimensional text baseline but do not significantly improve the full model. Company identity is the strongest driver of predicted redress, yet firm identity alone predicts far less well, and payment rail and bank response cues act in directions consistent with liability rules. Under assumed costs, thresholds selected on validation data substantially reduce modelled expected cost relative to standard thresholds, whereas model choice matters much less. Redress depends on both the firm and the facts that determine liability.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are enabling conversational agents capable of supporting increasingly complex workflows beyond traditional question-answering. In education, collaborative projects require continuous planning, coordination, and monitoring, yet existing educational chatbots mainly focus on tutoring or administrative support. This paper presents vProjTutor , an LLM-agent-based project management system that assists student teams throughout the complete project lifecycle. The proposed architecture integrates specialized LLM agents with external project-management tools, including Telegram, Trello, and GitHub, allowing users to configure projects, organize tasks, generate Sprint plans, monitor progress, and interpret repository activity through natural language interactions. A user study involving ten participants evaluated usability, task completion, and user satisfaction. Participants achieved an overall task completion rate of 93.3%, and the system obtained an overall BUS usability score of 85%. However, the system correctly interpreted 60% of commit messages, highlighting the need for further improvements in handling unstructured inputs. The results suggest that LLM-agent-based architectures constitute a promising approach for supporting collaborative projects in educational environments.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This literature review study aims to analyze the implementation of a student-centered learning (SCL) approach based on developmental psychology in Senior High Schools (SMA). High school-age adolescents (15–18 years) are at the formal-operational cognitive development stage and are undergoing an intensive identity formation phase. These psychological characteristics demand a learning approach that is not only content-centered but also responsive to the developmental dynamics of students. Through a systematic literature review of scientific sources published between 2020 and 2025, this study found that effective SCL implementation in high schools requires: (1) learning planning based on the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) and needs differentiation; (2) implementation integrating Problem-Based Learning, Project-Based Learning, and Cooperative Learning models; and (3) authentic assessment measuring holistic competence. Findings indicate that SCL grounded in developmental psychology understanding significantly enhances students' intrinsic motivation, cognitive-emotional engagement, and learning independence. Critical factors determining implementation success include teachers' pedagogical competence, institutional support, and the availability of a psychologically safe learning environment.

Ensuring high levels of Situation awareness (SA) is essential for air traffic controllers (ATCOs), enabling them to continuously process and integrate information into a comprehensive understanding of the situation as it dynamically changes. In the context of human-automation collaboration, SA becomes even more critical, as operators must be prepared to take over control in emergency situations. Although existing studies have largely assessed SA as either poor or good, limited research has explored identification of SA levels (Level 1, 2, and 3). To investigate the potential of eye-tracking technology for real-time SA levels assessment, we conducted an SA-inducing experiment involving 18 participants. Participants are required to perform a series of air traffic control (ATC) tasks corresponding to three SA levels, while their eye-tracking data were simultaneously collected. Eye-tracking features are analyzed using a two-way repeated measures ANOVA. Results identified total fixation duration, number of fixations, average pupil diameter and average amplitude of saccades as key indicators for distinguishing SA levels. Additionally, our findings highlight a significant interaction between SA levels and workload, demonstrating that the effectiveness of these metrics varies under different workload conditions. These insights contribute to enhancing real-time SA evaluation in the safety-critical environments like ATC, further improving the overall operational efficiency and safety in various human-automation collaboration scenarios.

Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines.

Are neural studies in psychology and neuroscience held to a lower standard of sample-size justification than behavioral studies, even when they use the same statistical tests? This registration specifies the confirmatory test of that claim. Exploratory findings. A large language model (Claude Opus 5.5), run with a fixed prompt, schema and codebook, screened 35,697 open-access articles published in 2025 in 308 JCR Q1 psychology and neuroscience journals and coded every eligible study's data type, main test, analyzed sample, stated minimum sample size and any justification of the sample size. Among 4,747 studies, neural studies stated a minimum sample size less often than behavioral studies and more often gave no justification of any kind. These findings rest on one automated measurement, checked so far only against itself; errors that differ between neural and behavioral studies could in principle produce them. Confirmatory test. Four human coders, blind to the model's codes, independently code a stratified random sample of 250 studies: 100 behavioral and 100 neural studies from the main analysis and 50 studies the model excluded from it. The sample is drawn by a registered rule and seed, studies are coded in random order, 50 studies are double-coded, and all coders first calibrate on 10 practice studies. We test (H1) whether neural studies still state a minimum less often and still more often give no justification after the full-sample rates are corrected for the coding errors measured against the human codes, and (H2) whether the automated coding agrees with human coding (κ ≥ .80; ICC ≥ .90 for sample size), a precondition for interpreting the full-sample results. Human codes are not treated as error-free: every disagreement is adjudicated. Expected outcomes. Corrected estimates of the two neural–behavioral gaps; agreement for each coded variable, overall and by data type; the model's error rates in each group; the rate at which the model wrongly excluded studies; and human–human reliability as a benchmark. If H1 holds, the gaps cannot be explained by coding error; if it fails, we will report that they cannot be distinguished from it. The pipeline, prompts, scripts and codes will be released openly for reuse and audit.
